How to play

Grave Wounds is a roleplaying game about small bands of fighting men and women in real wars, and about what wounds do to them. There are no hit points. A wound is a place on the body, the way it was made and how bad it is, and those three things decide whether it bleeds, hurts, stops a hand gripping or a leg bearing weight, and how long it would take to kill without help. Most wounds do not kill. They stop a fighter, and then the question is whether his friends can stop the bleeding, carry him to camp and keep the fever off.

What you need

  • Dice. Everything is rolled on d100: two ten-sided dice, one for tens and one for units, 01 to 00 (00 is 100). A few rolls use a single d10.
  • The pages. The wound roller, the team builder, the travel map and the field map run on any browser and keep your game in it. They roll the dice, look up the tables and keep the count, so the table can play quickly. Everything they do is written here, and the printed tables hold every table, so the game can be played on paper too.
  • A GM and players. One person runs the world and the enemy (the GM). Each player runs a team of four to six characters, not a single hero, so losing one is a loss and not the end of the evening.

The one roll

Every test is the same: roll d100, and equal to or under the number you are rolling against succeeds. That number is a skill or a characteristic, less any penalties. How far under you rolled is the margin, and in a fight the margin matters: a hit by a wide margin is a worse wound.

Out of a fight the GM calls for a roll only when failing would matter and the outcome is in doubt; a man with time and the right skill simply does the thing. The GM sets the difficulty:

Difficulty Modifier When
Easy +20 time to spare, good tools, a friendly or careless other side
Ordinary ±0 the usual way of things
Hard −20 in a hurry, at night, in a strange country or tongue, poor tools
Very hard −40 under fire, in the dark and the rain, against a man who expects it

A roll of 10% of the chance or under is a critical: the best result. A failed roll of 96 or more is a fumble: the worst.

One man against another. When someone resists (a sentry watching for a man sneaking past, a seller holding out on a price), both roll, the resisting side at Ordinary. The man acting wins only by beating them: a success over a failure, a critical over a plain success, or the wider margin between two of the same. A tie, or both failing, goes to the side resisting, and nothing changes. Where the GM has no sheet for the other side, it counts as 50.

The running example

This book follows one team from start to finish: a lord's retinue on the road to Towton in 1461, led by William of Ely. Each chapter picks up the story where the last left it: the team is made, Gilbert Cooper the archer shoots and is cut down, his friends stop the bleeding, and he is carried to camp to heal or die. The numbers in the example are the game's own; where a die is rolled, the book says what came up.

Time

The game's clock changes with what the team is doing:

Scale How long For
Round 6 seconds One action in a fight; bleeding; stop checks
Minute 10 rounds Binding wounds; the end of most fights
Day Marching, camps, the weather, sickness
Week Wounds healing in camp; catching disease
Season about 91 days Experience: ticked skills roll to rise

Characteristics and skills

Every character has six characteristics, from 15 to 95: Strength, Agility, Endurance, Wits, Nerve and Presence. Fifty is an ordinary person. Skills (Bow, Blade, Dodge, Leechcraft and the rest) start from a characteristic and grow with experience, up to 90. A character's attack is the skill his weapon is fought with, and his defence is the better of Parry and Dodge.

Using skills

What each skill and characteristic is for out of a fight, its usual difficulty, who resists it, and what follows (the GM decides when a case is easier or harder):

Skill Use Usually Against Success Failure Fumble
Persuade Haggle: Beat down a price. Ordinary the seller (Persuade) A tenth off (a quarter on a critical). The list price. No sale today.
Persuade Find a billet: Talk a village or a householder into a bed and a meal. Ordinary the householder or headman (Presence) Fed and bedded tonight: no keep to pay. He pays his keep, or sleeps rough. The village turns against the party: trouble.
Persuade Talk past a guard: Get by a sentry, a gate or the provost without the right papers. Hard the sentry or provost (Wits) Through. Turned back. Held as a deserter or a spy.
Persuade Question a prisoner: Get a prisoner or a local to talk. Ordinary the prisoner (Nerve) He tells what he knows (the GM decides how much is true). Nothing. He lies, and is believed.
Command Drive a hard task: Get men to do something hard and tiring: dig all night, march on after dark, cross a river. Ordinary — Done. Done slowly, or only half. They refuse.
Command Keep order: Stop plunder, drinking or a mutinous mood. Hard — They obey. Some slip away to it. They turn on him.
Letters Read or write: Read an order, a letter or a map's names; write a report. Easy — Read or written. Slowly, or with mistakes. He gets it wrong and does not know it.
Letters Forge a pass: Make a pass, an order or a billeting ticket that will be believed. Hard whoever checks it (Watch) It passes. Doubted: Talk past a guard instead. Seen through: held as a deserter or a spy.
Craft Mend kit: Mend a weapon, harness, boots, a cart or a radio set; a day's work. Ordinary — Mended. Not yet: another day. Ruined.
Craft Make something: Make ladders, a raft, a shelter, snowshoes or a litter from what is to hand. Ordinary — Made. Takes twice as long. It fails when it is used.
Ride Ride hard: Outride a pursuer, or catch a man who rides away. Ordinary the pursuer or the pursued (Ride) Away, or caught. Still close. Thrown: roll a fall as a wound.
Ride Swim a horse: Cross a deep ford or swim a river mounted. Hard — Across. Turned back. Swept away: Endurance check or drowned.
Seamanship Handle a boat: Take a boat across a river or along a coast; in rough water, hard. Ordinary — Across. Driven back. Swamped: Endurance check or drowned.
Fieldcraft Track: Follow men or animals. Ordinary the men being followed (Stealth) On their trail. Lost it. On the wrong trail.
Fieldcraft Find the way: Cross country without roads or a guide; at night, hard. Ordinary — On the way. Half a day lost. Lost: a day, or into the enemy.
Fieldcraft Hunt or gather: Find food or water for himself in the country. Ordinary — Fed today: no keep to pay. Nothing found. Something that makes him ill.
Watch Spot: See an ambush, a man hiding, a trap or a thing out of place. Ordinary whoever is hiding (Stealth) Seen. Missed. Sure there is nothing there.
Watch Search: Search a house, a body or a baggage wagon. Easy — Found what there is. Missed it. Missed it and left traces.
Stealth Sneak: Get past sentries, into a camp or away from one. Ordinary the sentries (Watch) Unseen. Seen, but not yet caught. Walks into them.
Stealth Steal: Lift a purse, a horse or rations unseen. Hard the owner or the guard (Watch) Taken. Not taken. Caught in the act: the provost.
Leechcraft Diagnose: Tell what a sick man has, and whether it will spread. Ordinary — Named: the GM tells which sickness. Unsure. Wrong.
Strength Force or carry: Force a door, lift a beam, carry a wounded man. Ordinary — Done. Not alone. Strained: a step of fatigue.
Agility Climb or jump: Climb a wall, jump a ditch, keep his feet on ice. Ordinary — Over. Not this way. Falls: roll a fall as a wound.
Endurance Endure: Keep going: swim, go without sleep, hold out in the cold. Ordinary — Holds out. A step of fatigue. Collapses, or goes under.
Wits Notice or remember: Recall a face, a road or a password; work something out. Ordinary — Yes. No. Remembers it wrong.
Nerve Keep his head: Stay calm out of a fight: under shelling in a dugout, at a hanging, before an officer. Ordinary — Steady. Shaken: −10 to his next check. Breaks: runs, freezes or lashes out.
Presence Impress: Stare a man down, make a first impression, be remembered. Ordinary the other man (Presence) He gives way. No effect. Made an enemy.

Haggling. Buying from the price list, a man may haggle: his Persuade against the seller's (50). If he wins he pays 10% less (25% on a critical); if not, the list price; and if he fumbles the seller will not deal with him today.

A skill check that succeeds (or wins against someone) ticks the skill for experience; a characteristic is not ticked. A hurt man checks worse: out of a fight a check (a job's included) takes the same penalty his attack would in the roller, from pain, blood lost, wounds, fatigue (a hungry day is a step of it), sickness and Strain; with no fight to go by, his Strain alone.

Selling and hiring. Loot that is goods (not money, prize money or a ransom) may be sold haggling: his Persuade against the buyer's; a win gets 10% more (25% on a critical), a fumble lets a fence cheat him of 25%. A man hiring a replacement may haggle his price as at the price list; on a fumble the man will not sign today.

Tongues

A man speaks his own tongue at 90, which never changes (Letters is the separate skill of reading and writing). Any other is a figure read in bands:

Figure Reads as
0 none
1-25 a few words
26-50 getting by
51-75 conversation
76+ fluent

A tongue he lacks he knows at a share of a related one he has (half of German from Low German, three quarters of English from Scots). Pidgins rise no higher than 35 (Bamboo English in Korea, GI Vietnamese), the Plains sign language no higher than 75, and a learned tongue no higher than 85.

Talking in a tongue. Persuade and Command in another tongue are at most his figure in it: a fine talker with twenty words of French is a man with twenty words of French.

Words across tongues. An order to a man of another tongue, a call on a foe to surrender (or his own surrender), a question to a prisoner or a villager: d100 at the best tongue the two share (the lower of their figures). A critical is understood in full; a success, understood; a failure, only the gist (an order half done, a surrender not understood); a fumble, a dangerous error, the wrong thing understood (at the Grattan fight of 1854 a drunk interpreter's broken Lakota began a war; in Afghanistan "fire an illume" was heard as "fire mortars"). From the Crimea on, armies issued phrase books: a yes or no, a number or a pointed direction is then Easy at no worse than 25.

Passing as a native. His figure against the listener's Watch (both roll): Ordinary in his own tongue, Hard fluent without the idiom (76+), Very hard a good speaker (51-75), and below that he cannot pass. In 1944 Skorzeny found ten men with perfect English and idiom for Operation Greif, thirty or forty good speakers, and over a hundred moderate ones; those caught in American uniform were shot.

Taken and escaping. A man who asks for quarter in his captors' tongue is a little safer (the capture roll is 10 better: a surrender had to be accepted to protect him). Escaping, his Fieldcraft to get home is +10 if he converses in their tongue and +20 if it is his own.

On the travel map the people where a force stands speak a tongue, or in mixed country several: those of the nearest town, village or landmark within 6 miles (10 km) that names its own, else the map's. A force with no named man who gets by in any of them forages Hard, its talk is in the best of them he has, and a month among them ticks their main tongue. The map shows a place's tongues when you point at it.

Learning. A tongue used well is ticked and rolls to rise at End of season like a skill (one at 0 always rises). A month among its speakers on the travel map, or a season held prisoner, ticks it; so does a week with a language master, a teammate who speaks it well, or (from 1943) an army course. The army's courses took three months for the better students to order a meal or rent a room; the Foreign Legion's recruits answered in French within ten days.

Interpreters. The team may hire an interpreter for a season: a man of the other army who speaks the team's tongue and his own at 50 to 85 (rolled). He costs 1 Day a day (0.4 for the modern wars, where Iraqi interpreters began at $600 a month in 2005). A man who talks through him uses the interpreter's figure in that tongue, not his own. Of those hired 28% are unreliable (a whistleblower said 28% of one firm's Afghan hires failed the language standard): his roll of 90 or more is a dangerous error. Each End of season he may be killed (0.5%, 1% in the modern wars: in Iraq some fifteen times a US soldier's rate), and his season is up. On the travel map, where the people speak his tongue and the team's named men march with the force, he forages and talks for it: the force does not forage Hard for want of the tongue, and its billeting and talk go through him at his figure.

Age

Enlisting. A man enlists at his era's starting age, raised to his army's legal least (15 to 60 under the Statute of Winchester; 17 to 25 for Victorian recruits; 18 to 37 in the American draft of 1942). Then d100: a few are boys under age (about a tenth of the Union army was under 18), enlisted at up to 3 years below the least, and a few older recruits, from 38 up to 6 years past the most (over it, he lied). A man under or over age is found out at 10% each End of season and sent home, until he is of age (a boy) or has served out his first term (an older man). Most characters are made after their terms, so a boy's lie matters only in the eras of one-year terms. A recruit who enlisted at 38 or more takes 2 times the Wear for his service: Union men enlisting at about 39 had 1.8 times the odds of dying of disease of men of 20 in their first year, and 2.4 after.

A man ages with his terms. For every 4 years of his life past the start of his service (at the making of a character, the years of his terms; in play, each term served) he rolls his age band's decline, taken from his characteristics as a lasting hurt is (his skills that rest on them fall with them), and, from 20, gains a step of maturity: +1 Presence and +1 Nerve until 40, +1 Wits until 45 (at most +5 each). Each promotion adds +2 Presence, to +6 in all (a design estimate: a man who leads grows into it). Endurance goes first, then Agility, then Strength; Wits slows from 50:

Age (middle of the 4 years) Strength Agility Endurance Wits
30–39 — −d3 −d2 —
40–49 −d3 −d4 −d4 —
50–59 −d4 −d6 −d6 −d2
60 and over −d6 −2d4 −2d4 −d2

Wear. Service wears a man: +1 Wear for each 4 years, and +1 for each hard season (a month of hard nights on the travel map, hungry, sick or wounded, or colder and wetter than his shelter; or the GM's word for a siege, a famine or a tropical station). Each 4 Wear makes him 2 years older for his decline, and from 6 Wear his Endurance rolls twice and takes the worse.

Worn out. For each term he serves from 35, or with 8 Wear or more, he rolls d100: at or under 3 × Wear + 2 × (his age − 35) − (Endurance − 50) ÷ 2, he is worn out (a 1-year term rolls a quarter of that). From 40, Endurance under 30, or Strength, Agility or Endurance under 25, wears him out at once. The GM may send him home (with a pension where his army gave one) or keep him on. British soldiers discharged "worn out" were mostly 41 to 44, after 21 to 25 years.

Experience

Training. A skill can also be ticked by a week's teaching: from a master for hire where the team is (a riding master, a master of defence, a schoolmaster, a surgeon, a craftsman; his skill counts as 60, and he charges a fee by the week), or from a teammate at least 20 better (who gives up the week too). The teacher rolls his skill; a success ticks the pupil's skill, a failure wastes the week. The pupil pays the fee and his keep; a teammate who teaches loses the week from his next job term. An army drills its men: a week in which a force its army feeds spent four days or more not marching, the best Command with it (or the army's own sergeants, 50) rolls, and on a success each named man's weapon skill is ticked. Riding lessons in London in 1879 cost about six days of a private's pay each; the other fees are estimates.

Courses. Some training takes him away for weeks or a year, for set gains: a year as an apprentice or in a knight's household, two weeks at a Civil War camp of instruction, eighteen months at Sandhurst, four and a half at a 1916 officer cadet battalion, seventeen weeks at an American Officer Candidate School (22 in Korea, 23 in Vietnam, 12 today), Ranger School, the Special Forces course. An army's course counts as service, and an officer's course makes him eligible for its rank at the next vacancy, whatever his rank and years:

Course Eras Away Gains
A year as an apprentice Medieval, Thirty Years' War, Horse and musket, Crimean War, Civil War and frontier 52 weeks craft +10, letters +2
A year in a knight's household (page or squire) Medieval 52 weeks blade +5, ride +5, command +3, letters +2
Royal Military College, Sandhurst (about 18 months) Horse and musket, Crimean War 78 weeks command +10, letters +5, gunnery +3; opens ensign
A camp of instruction (about two weeks of drill) Civil War and frontier 2 weeks rifle +5, bayonet +3
An officer cadet battalion (4½ months, from 1916) First World War 19 weeks command +10, letters +3, signals +2; opens lieutenant
Officer Candidate School (17 weeks) Second World War 17 weeks command +10, letters +3, signals +2; opens lieutenant
Officer Candidate School (22 weeks) Korean War 22 weeks command +10, letters +3, signals +2; opens lieutenant
Officer Candidate School (23 weeks) Vietnam War 23 weeks command +10, letters +3, signals +2; opens lieutenant
Officer Candidate School (12 weeks) The Falklands to Afghanistan 12 weeks command +10, letters +3, signals +2; opens lieutenant
Royal Military Academy Sandhurst (44 weeks) The Falklands to Afghanistan 44 weeks command +12, letters +3, signals +2; opens lieutenant
Ranger School (about 9 weeks) Korean War, Vietnam War, The Falklands to Afghanistan 9 weeks fieldcraft +8, stealth +5, command +3
Special Forces Qualification Course (a year or more) Vietnam War, The Falklands to Afghanistan 56 weeks fieldcraft +8, signals +8, leechcraft +5, stealth +5

A skill used well is ticked: a job's check that succeeds (lawful or not; a failed or fumbled check, or a job with no check, teaches nothing), a hit, a parry or dodge that works, first aid that works, Fieldcraft that finds fresh food on the march, a week nursing the sick (the best Leechcraft with the force), Stealth that surprises an enemy and Watch that stops one surprising his. A skill is ticked once however often it is used. At the end of a season (about 91 days, when the GM calls it) each ticked skill rolls d100: over the skill, it rises 1-3, never past 90; then the ticks clear. Low skills rise quickly and high ones slowly.

Time served. Days at a job with a skill check (not fumbled) and every day with a force on the travel map count toward a term, as long as one of his career terms (4 years in most eras). Each term served gives a later term's gains (10 to his career's main skill and 5 to its second) and its years of age, at the next end of season, and rolls on his career's term table as at the making of a character: its event (+15 to its skill, and a line of his story) and its wound chance (a scar, or a lasting hurt). His starting purse is not changed.

Anyone without a sheet (a bystander, an enemy the GM has not written up) counts as 50 in every characteristic, and fights at his quality:

Quality Attack Defence Nerve
Green 40% 25% 35
Regular 50% 35% 50
Veteran 60% 45% 65

For the GM

Quality is the quickest way to make an enemy: decide whether he is green, regular or veteran, and the table gives his attack, defence and Nerve. The followers of the players' teams use the same table, and so do whole units on the field map.

Making a team

A team is four to six characters with a shared history: a lord's retinue, a free company, a patrol. The first character leads it, and when he falls another steps up. The team builder makes a whole team in one click, or one character at a time, from the tables of 11 eras; the printed tables hold the same tables for the table top. This chapter uses the medieval tables (c.1250–1460). The other eras follow the same five steps with their own careers, skills and kit (Other wars).

The five steps

1. Characteristics. Roll 3d6 × 5 for each characteristic in order (15 to 90), or take the fixed array 70, 60, 55, 50, 45, 35 and place it, highest first, where the character's career wants it most.

2. Origin. Roll d100 on the origin table (20 origins). It says where he comes from, gives one skill +15, and a trait and a drawback that go together: a characteristic ±10 or a skill ±15.

3. Career terms. The leader serves three terms, the others one or two. In each term:

  • his career's main skill rises, +15 in the first term and +10 after;
  • its second skill rises +5;
  • d100 on the career's table gives an event, and the skill it taught rises +15. An event he has had already moves to the next row down.

He starts at 16 and is 4 years older for each term. Nobody dies while being made. The 13 medieval careers:

Career Main skill Second skill
Man-at-arms Blade Parry
Archer Bow Dodge
Crossbowman Crossbow Dodge
Spearman or billman Polearm Parry
Mounted sergeant Ride Parry
Mercenary Axe and mace Parry
Sailor Seamanship Dodge
Clerk or priest Letters Persuade
Barber-surgeon Leechcraft Craft
Forester or huntsman Fieldcraft Stealth
Servant or groom Ride Watch
Merchant Persuade Letters
Townswoman or castle household at a siege Craft Watch

4. Old wounds. A term marked * on its table (a siege, a broken line, a rout) leaves an old wound, and so does a d100 at or under the career's wound chance. Its place is rolled on the region's own wound table, the same one the roller uses. Then d100: up to 70, a healed scar; above, a lasting hurt, 5 off the characteristic that place governs (Wits for the head, Presence for the face, Strength for the arms, Agility for the legs, Endurance for the body).

5. Skills and kit. Each skill starts at a characteristic divided by 2, 3, 4 or 5 (rounded down), plus what he gained, to 90 at most. His kit and weapon come with his first career and his region.

Money. A Day is a common soldier's day's pay in his army's coin: 6d for an English archer. Each character starts with 30 Days saved for each career term, so a leader of three terms has 90 Days (£2 5s). His issued kit and weapon cost him nothing; the team builder shows what they are worth in Days. In camp, a man who spends a day of rest earning money gets 1 Day for it; one who takes a job does better or worse by the job (Finding work). What he earns goes into his purse and what he buys or pays comes out of it, at the era's prices in Days; he cannot spend more than he has. Away from an army that feeds him, his keep comes out of it too (Keep).

Losses. A man killed, dead of wounds or disease, taken prisoner, deserted or sent home leaves the team. First his purse is settled as his era did it: shared among his comrades (a frontier outfit, an insurgent cell), sent to his heirs (by his will in the Middle Ages, through the regiment's judge in the Thirty Years' War, and by the articles of war after), or lost with him (the Plains nations gave a dead man's things away); the GM may choose otherwise. Then the gap is filled one of three ways: a new man rolled like any other, of the lost man's career and terms; a man assigned by the army through its own system (a draft from the depot, a replacement depot, a new man on a twelve-month tour), free but green and only after a wait of days; or a man hired where the team is (a mercenary, a substitute, a contractor), at a price in Days from a purse, more for a veteran. If the leader is lost, the man with the most terms left leads.

The retinue: Gilbert Cooper

The team builder rolls a lord's retinue from England: William of Ely, a man-at-arms, leads it. Its senior archer is Gilbert Cooper, 2 terms, age 24: Strength 35, Agility 60, Endurance 50, Wits 56, Nerve 21, Presence 21. He was novice who left the cloister (knows his herbs; faints at the sight of blood), and in his terms he fought hand to hand when the line broke and ran from a charge of horse and lived. His skills that matter here: Bow 55, Dodge 45, Fieldcraft 18, Stealth 20. He fights with the longbow at 55%, and his defence is 45%.

His Endurance is low, and it shows in a fight: his Blood is 20, not the usual 20 (next chapter). With Agility 60 he rolls d10 + 6 for initiative.

Followers

A big team's other men get no sheet, only a line: a career, a name and a quality, rolled on d100. The quality gives their attack, defence and Nerve (the table in How to play). Some teams roll on a better or worse table:

Quality table Green Regular Veteran
Default 01–30 31–80 81–00
Hardened 01–15 16–60 61–00
Raw 01–55 56–90 91–00

For the GM

Followers are what make a team feel like a household or a company, and they are who dies first. Name them; the players will remember them. On the field map they fight as units around the team, who go with them as heroes.

The fight

A fight runs in rounds of 6 seconds. Each round every fighter who can act takes one turn, in order of initiative; then the round ends, the wounded bleed and the sides check their nerve. Most fights last a minute or two: one side breaks long before it is all down.

The wound roller runs all of this: pick an attacker and a defender, roll the hit, apply it, and press Next fighter and Next round. Its battle map is a grid of hexes about 2 yards (2 m) across.

A fighter's turn

  1. Initiative. At the start of the fight each fighter rolls d10 + Agility ÷ 10 (rounded down), and they act from highest to lowest. A fighter who is down, out of the fight, or on a side that has broken does not act.
  2. Move or stay. He may stay, advance up to 4 hexes and still attack, or run up to 12 hexes and not attack. He may pass through friends but not stop on them. Leaving an enemy's side by more than one step gives that enemy a free attack.
  3. Attack. Roll d100 against his attack, less his wound penalties and any range penalty. Equal or under hits, and the margin is how far under. A roll at or under a tenth of the chance is a critical: it cannot be defended.
  4. Defence. The defender may roll d100 against his defence (Parry or Dodge), less his own penalties. Equal or under, the blow misses.
  5. Where it lands. Roll d100 on the era's hit-location table for the place, and on the weapon's table for how it wounds: a cut, a thrust (pierce), a crushing blow, a bullet.
  6. How bad. The margin sets the severity: under 20 light, from 20 serious, from 50 (or on a critical) critical. Firearms have their own bands for the body and the limbs. A hit by a margin of 2 or less, if it is not a critical, only grazes: its bleeding and pain are a step less, and it calls for no stop check.
  7. Armour. The armour on that place lowers the severity a step at a time against that kind of blow, if its coverage roll says the blow met it. Some weapons are made to beat armour: a war bow's heavy arrows go through mail and a jack as if they were not there.
  8. The wound. Look up the wound for the place, the kind of blow and the severity, and write it down. Its effects are in the next chapter.
  9. The stop check. A serious and critical wound that carries shock (most do; many limb wounds do not) calls for a d100 against the wounded man's Nerve, less his pain and blood-loss penalties, and 10 more for a critical wound:
Result He is Which means
Equal or under Fighting on No change
Failed by 1–20 Defend only for 2 rounds No attack; he may move and defend
Failed by 21–40 Stunned for 2 rounds No attack; −50% to his defence
Failed by more than 40 Out of the fight until helped or the fight ends Takes no part: no attack, no defence

A worse result replaces a milder one, and the round it happens in is the first of its rounds. This is what ends real fights: men stop, sit down, crawl away, long before they die.

The retinue: the arrow

On the road to Towton the retinue meets a band of Lancastrian billmen, regulars. It is Gilbert Cooper's turn, and the nearest billman is in short range. He shoots at 55% and rolls 21: a hit by a margin of 34, serious. The billman tries to dodge at 35% and rolls 61: no. The arrow strikes his chest (left), a thrust. His jack would take the wound down 1 step, but the war bow's arrows ignore it, so it stays serious: bleeding 2, pain 2, short of breath, and it would kill in hours untreated. It carries shock, so he makes a stop check: Nerve 50, less 2 steps of pain, gives 30. He rolls 47, failing by 17: he can defend only for 2 rounds.

The retinue: the bill

The billmen close. One reaches Gilbert and swings at 50%, rolling 22: a margin of 28, serious. Gilbert dodges at 45% and rolls 58. The bill opens his thigh (right), a cut, where his jack does not reach. The wound bleeds 3 (arterial), pain 2, and the leg is hurt. It does not carry shock, so there is no stop check, and he fights on. But at 3 Blood a round, his 20 Blood will be gone in 6 rounds. The next chapter is about what that means.

The end of the round

  • Bleeding. Every wounded fighter loses Blood at his wounds' rate (next chapter).
  • Results wear off. Defend only and stunned count down a round.
  • Pain. A fighter whose pain is above the cap (3 steps, −30%) makes a stop check every round, as for a serious wound.
  • Morale. A side with 25% or more of its fighters down rolls d100 against the best Nerve among those still up (its leader's, if he is up): +10 while a leader is up, and (Presence − 50) ÷ 5 more for him; −20 if a leader is down; −20 once 50% of the side is down. Over the target, the side breaks: it runs or surrenders.

For the GM

The roller asks for the stop check and the morale roll when they are due, and you can type your own dice into it. Remember that most enemies want to live too: a side that breaks runs, and a man who is down asks for quarter. A fight is usually decided in a minute.

Wounds and movement

A leg wound halves a fighter's move (advance 2, run 6). A man who has collapsed or cannot stand crawls 1 hex. A winded man cannot run, and a stunned or out man cannot move at all. The printed tables and the roller's battle map have the rest: ground, height, cover, works and weather.

Wounds

A wound is written down as what it does. Each one has five things, and they add up across all of a fighter's wounds:

  • Bleeding, from B0 (none) to B3 (arterial).
  • Pain, from P0 to P3.
  • Impairments: what the wound stops the body doing.
  • Shock, fracture or severed: shock calls for the stop check; a fracture is a bone that needs setting; a severed part is gone.
  • The clock: how long it would take to kill him untreated, from none through days, hours, minutes and rounds to instant.

Blood

Every fighter has a Blood pool: 20, plus (Endurance − 50) ÷ 10, rounded down (16 at Endurance 15, 24 at 95). Each wound bleeds away Blood at its rate:

Bleed Blood lost What it is
B0 none None
B1 1 a minute Slow: seeping; lose 1 Blood per minute
B2 1 a round Heavy: lose 1 Blood per round; bind within minutes
B3 3 a round Arterial: lose 3 Blood per round; tourniquet or pressure now

As Blood falls, so does the fighter:

Blood left Effect
75% or less Pale and weak: -10% to all actions
50% or less Faint check each minute; -20% to all actions
25% or less Barely conscious: -40% to all actions, can only crawl
None Unconscious and dying

Bleeding is what kills quickly. A man with an arterial wound has a few rounds; a man with a heavy one has a few minutes; slow bleeding gives his friends time.

Penalties

A wounded fighter fights worse. Add up:

  • Pain: −10% to attack and defence for each step, counted to 3 steps at most (and above that, a stop check every round).
  • Blood lost: the table above.
  • Impairments, each counted once however many wounds cause it. An arm's impairment counts against his weapon arm (his weapon hand's side) or his shield arm (the other):
Impairment What it does Attack Defence
Dazed Stunned: lose next action, then -20% for 1d6 rounds −20% −20%
Vision Vision impaired: -30% to sight-based actions; blinded if both eyes −30% −30%
Breath Winded: no sustained exertion; fatigue doubled −10% −10%
Collapse Collapses; can only crawl or crouch −20% −30%
Stand Falls and cannot stand unaided −20% −30%
Leg Movement halved; -20% to footwork and dodging — −20%
Move Movement halved — −10%
Unconscious Knocked out (check each minute to wake) — —
Speech Cannot speak clearly — —
Arm (weapon arm) That arm -20%; no two-handed use −20% —
Arm (shield arm) That arm -20%; no two-handed use — −10%
Grip (weapon arm) Drops anything held in that hand; cannot grip with it −30% —
Grip (shield arm) Drops anything held in that hand; cannot grip with it — —
Hand useless (weapon arm) That hand useless −30% —
Hand useless (shield arm) That hand useless — —
Arm useless (weapon arm) That arm useless −40% —
Arm useless (shield arm) That arm useless — −10%

Attack and defence penalties are each capped at −60%. A fighter with no usable hand cannot hold a weapon. A fighter with either arm hurt (an arm wound, a lost grip, a useless hand or arm) cannot attack with a two-handed weapon (bows, crossbows, long guns, bills, pikes and poleaxes): he can only defend until he takes up something he can use in one hand.

First aid

A wound can be treated three ways (on the roller, the buttons on the casualty's card). How long it takes, and whether anyone can reach him under fire, is the GM's call:

  • Bind: pressure and a bandage, one step less bleeding.
  • Tourniquet: an arm or a leg only; the bleeding stops. Left on for hours, the limb is lost.
  • Cauterise: the bleeding stops, at one more step of pain.

If anyone on his side comes from the team builder, the best Leechcraft among them still standing rolls d100 for each treatment. Success: a bind stops 2 steps instead of one, and cautery adds no pain. Failure: nothing happens, and it can be tried again next turn. A side with no sheets binds without rolling.

The retinue: the tourniquet

Gilbert's thigh bleeds 3 Blood a round. The best Leechcraft in the retinue is not its barber-surgeon's but Nicholas Fletcher's, the barber-surgeon: 32. He drags Gilbert back and tries a tourniquet; he rolls 41, over his 32, and the strap slips. He tries again the next round and rolls 19: it holds, and the bleeding stops. Two rounds of bleeding have left Gilbert 14 of 20 Blood: pale and weak.

His wound penalties now: pain 2 and the Blood he lost give −30% to attack; his hurt leg adds to his defence, −50%. He moves at half pace. He is out of this fight in all but name, and alive.

For the GM

The clock is a guide to the story, not a timer to run down: a wound fatal in hours is one that needs a surgeon tonight, not one that kills on the stroke of the hour. Blood is what the rules count. A man who reaches no Blood is unconscious and dying; what happens next is first aid, luck, and the camp.

Recovery

After the fight come the days that decide who lives. Wounds, sickness and fever all move on one track of five steps, and each step weakens a man in the next fight:

Step In a fight
Healed —
Mending −10% to attack and defence
Serious −25% to attack and defence, cannot run
Grave −25% to attack and defence, crawls only, defends only
Deadly too ill to fight

Into camp

Each wound goes onto the track at the step its severity gives (light mending, serious serious, critical grave), or worse if its clock is short: a wound that would kill in hours or minutes starts at grave. In camp the bleeding stops, and each night he gets back 4 Blood.

On the wound roller, put him With his force on the travel map and press To camp; the travel map's nights then run his wounds with the force's own wounded.

The recovery check

Once every 7 days, each wound makes a recovery check: d100 against his Endurance, adjusted:

What To the roll
Care: no camp -20
Care: a camp +0
Care: quarters in houses +10
He marched that day -20
He rested +10
A night harder than the shelter (cold, wet) -10
Poor hygiene -10
A leech with the force + his Leechcraft ÷ 10
Battle wounds heal easily +20
Wound fever is hard −25
  • Succeed by 30 or more: two steps better.
  • Succeed: one step better.
  • Fail: it holds; at deadly, he dies.
  • Fail by 30 or more: one step worse.

A wound that reaches healed leaves a scar on his sheet and figure.

Wound fever

3 to 5 days after the fight, each wound turns septic or it does not: 5% for a wound with a low risk of infection, 15% medium, 30% high; +5 with no camp, −5 in quarters, less a leech's bonus. A septic wound is wound fever: a step worse, checked every night, and the check is harder by 25. Before antibiotics, this is what killed the men who survived the battle.

The retinue: the camp

The retinue carries Gilbert to its camp. His wound goes onto the track at serious. A few nights on, its risk of fever is 12% (medium, less 3 for Nicholas Fletcher's Leechcraft). The GM rolls 64: it stays clean.

At the end of the week he checks: Endurance 50, a camp (+0), resting (+10), a leech (+3) and a battle wound (+20) make 83. He rolls 52, a success by 31: one step better, mending. A week later he rolls 30, a success by 53: healed, with a scar on his right thigh. His Blood came back in his first nights in camp, and the retinue marches on with its archer.

For the GM

The track is where the campaign's hard choices are made. March on, and every check is -20; camp in the open, and fever is likelier; stay in a filthy camp, and the flux comes. The travel map counts all of it for whole forces; the players only have to decide.

Strain

Fighting wears on a man's mind as well as his body. Strain builds from what he goes through:

What Strain
A light day in the line (patrols, sniping) +0.5
A day in the line (holding, regular shelling) +1
A fight (an attack, a defence, a bombardment) +2
An extreme day (street fighting, the bocage, a storm) +3
A comrade killed or maimed +4
His side lost a quarter or more +3
His leader killed +3
His trusted leader killed +6
Wounded +2
Badly wounded +3
A near miss, buried by a shell +2
A hard sight or deed +2
Two days without sleep, cold and wet +1
A season in captivity +1
A season in a harsh camp +2

A day in the line, a fight or an extreme day is changed by how he stands with his comrades, summed: | | Strain | |---|---| | A trusted leader | -25% | | Comrades of long standing | -25% | | A replacement among strangers | +25% | | On the move (an advance or a withdrawal) | -50% |

and 40% of every point also goes into his Toll, which only going home lowers. Each time Strain and Toll together pass 10, 20, 30 and on, he rolls d100: at or under his Nerve + 115 − that total, he holds; a man who has broken down before rolls 10 less. If he fails, he rolls d10, adding 1 for each 10 he failed by: 1-4 shaken (−10 to attack and Nerve until a day's rest), 5-7 strained (−20 until treated), 8-9 broken down (out of the fight until treated), 10 or more severely (out, and to be sent back). Each era has its own words for these: nostalgia in the Napoleonic and Civil wars, shell shock in 1914-18, combat exhaustion in 1944.

A day out of the line, camped, takes 3.5 Strain off. A man who breaks down is treated where he is, near the front or in the rear; the nearer and the sooner, the likelier he goes back to duty:

Where Days Back to duty: shaken strained broken down severely
With his unit (comrades, a sergeant, a priest) 2 60% 60% 30% 10%
A forward exhaustion centre (from 1916) 3 70% 65% 60% 30%
A hospital in the rear 14 50% 40% 30% 20%
Sent home 60 30% 20% 13% 10%
Furlough home (before 1914) 30 60% 50% 40% 30%

Except treatment with his unit, he is away from the force for those days: the travel map counts them off, and he comes back to it when they are done. If the team's leader is killed, each of his men takes the Strain of it (3), twice that if he was a trusted leader (Command 60 or more): a design estimate, since no study measured it.

Korea, Vietnam and the later wars rotated men home at the end of a tour: Strain gone, the Toll cut to a quarter. For the Plains nations, a homecoming that welcomes and honours a man halves it. A man who ends a campaign with his Toll at or above his Nerve, or who broke down, may carry a lasting effect: the GM notes it as part of who he is (sleeping badly, starting at noises, drinking, grief), never as a penalty.

For the GM

These rules follow the US Army's figures of 1944: a man of ordinary Nerve in a rifle company lasted about 80 to 90 days of combat, and nearly every man had broken down by 200 to 240 days; British units, rested every twelve days, lasted about twice as long. Breaking down was not weakness: it came to almost everyone who stayed in the line long enough. Handle it with the respect the men who lived it deserve.

Battles of hundreds

When hundreds fight, rolling for every man every round would take all night. On the field map the rank and file fight as units, resolved a minute at a time through the same wound tables, and the team fights among them as heroes with the full rules of the fight.

The field map

The field map is a grid of hexes 11 yards (10 m) across. One exchange is about a minute, some 10 rounds. Each exchange, one side moves, then the other, and then every melee and volley is resolved at once.

A unit is a block of hexes: its front row along its line, its men in rows behind. It has a number of men, a quality (green, regular or veteran, as in How to play), a weapon, armour and a formation:

Formation Men a hex Abreast Ranks Move (hexes) Shots at it count
Close order 40 10 4 6 ×1
Open order 20 10 2 8 ×0.8
Battery 20 4 5 6 ×0.8
Extended order 3 3 1 8 ×0.5
Machine-gun team 5 5 1 4 ×0.5
Anti-tank guns 5 1 1 2 ×0.5

Mounted units move 15 hexes. A unit that ends its move touching the enemy may have come up to 2 times its move: a charge. A unit in contact cannot move. Units cannot pass through each other, except that a steady unit charging may pass through its own side's men to reach the enemy; the units it passes through lose half their move that exchange.

Seeing. To aim, to lay a gun on a target or to call fire, a man must see it. Woods and buildings between block his sight unless they stand lower than he does; he sees 1 hex into them, and out of them from their edge. Ground between that stands higher than both him and his target is dead ground: a rise hides each from the other. A crest within 1 hex of either man does not count, so a man or a tank pulled up just behind it sees over it and is seen, and a man on the top sees down both slopes.

An exchange

  1. Who strikes. In melee, the front rank of each hex touching the enemy, and one more rank for each hex of the weapon's reach past the first (spears and bills strike from two ranks, the pike from three). With missiles, the men who have the target in range.
  2. How many blows tell. Most of a minute in a press is shoving and watching for an opening: about one striking man in 11 makes a real attempt each exchange. A longbowman looses 8 arrows a minute, and about one shot in 30 is aimed at a man rather than loosed at the mass.
  3. Each attempt is one attack, at the unit's quality, exactly as in the fight: +20 from the flank, +30 from the rear (and no parry), +20 for a mounted charge in its first exchange, −10 for a shaken unit, +20 for pikes in close order against horse to their front; range, weather and cover come off missiles. A tired unit loses its fatigue level's penalty off its attack and its parry.
  4. The wound is rolled as for one man. A light wound or a graze: he fights on. Serious or critical: a stop check, and failing it puts him down. A wound that kills within rounds kills. Against modern fire (breech-loaders on, machine guns, shell, grenades), every serious or critical wound puts him down and a light one calls for the check: the casualty returns from 1914 on count nearly every man hit as out of the line.
  5. Morale, below; then the next exchange.

Fatigue. A unit tires as a character does. Each exchange it fights hand to hand counts one toil, and so does each hex it goes in deep mud or snow. After 12 toil in heavy armour, 20 in medium, or 30 in light, it is a fatigue step worse, to Exhausted at most, and stays so for the battle. Shooting costs none, and vehicles don't tire.

Quick-play blows (a GM's choice). Rolling every blow is exact but slow on a table. To roll a group's blows in one go: count the tries as above, then find the men down per 100 tries in the era's quick-play chart (in the tables) for the weapon against the target's armour, at the attack after all modifiers, times the quality factor printed with it, times (1 − parry × 0.9) if the target can parry. Tries × that ÷ 100 is the average; roll d100 on the spread chart for the men down. The field page's Quick-play sheet prints the exact figures for the units on the field, and ticking quick-play blows makes the page roll this way too. Blows that fall on a hero are still rolled one at a time. It gives the same losses on average, with the same spread, as rolling every blow. Shellfire goes the same way (see fire support): one roll for one battery's fire on one unit.

Morale and the rout

After an exchange a unit checks its morale if it lost the exchange in contact (more of its men down than it put down), has 25% of its men down, lost 10% of its men in this exchange, or was struck in the flank or rear. A unit holding its ground in a position (in a bunker, dug in, behind works, in buildings or rubble, or lying down in woods or scrub), not flanked, counts its losses only in an exchange it lost men: a garrison does not break from the passing of time. It rolls d100 against its quality's Nerve:

Modifier
Still steady, ranks closed +20
A named leader with it, up +10
Its leader down −20
Half its men down −20
Struck in flank or rear −20
A steady friendly unit beside it +10
Dug in: gone to ground or in a bunker +10
Lost the exchange −5 a man more lost than it put down (at most −30)
  • Steady, fails: it is shaken: it fights at −10 and cannot charge. Failing by more than 20 while flanked, or with half its men down, it breaks at once.
  • Shaken, fails: it breaks.
  • Shaken, passes out of contact: it rallies to steady.

A broken unit runs. Every enemy man in reach strikes it at +20, with no parry and twice as often, as long as the pursuers keep up. This is where most of a battle's dead fell, as at Towton and Agincourt, where the beaten side lost far more men in flight than in the press.

On the field map it runs straight back as far as it can move. Its own side's units do not stop it: it runs on through them to the first clear ground beyond, and each unit it runs through loses half its move that exchange as the fugitives push through its ranks.

For the GM

A melee of ten or twenty minutes, decided by morale more than by wounds, with the beaten side losing most of its men in the rout: that is the shape the records show, and the page is tuned to give it. Let the players' heroes break a line rather than kill it.

Ammunition

A unit that shoots carries only so much. Its load is counted in exchanges of fire: the rounds, arrows or bolts a man carries (a machine gun's belts, for a gun), over the rate it fires at, times 30% (men do not fire every round they could). Longbowmen have about 20 exchanges of shooting, riflemen of 1914-53 about 40, a machine gun about 22. Vehicles and guns count their own rounds.

  • Running low. Each exchange it shoots uses one. At 25% of a full load or less it shoots at half rate; with none it cannot shoot at all, still fights hand to hand, and has -10 on morale.
  • Resupply. An exchange out of contact, neither moving nor firing, within 5 hexes of a supply source: its side's map edge (behind the way most of its men face), a lorry or armoured carrier of its side, or a supply dump. The GM places dumps before the battle; from the Second World War on, an air drop called on a side's move lands as a dump at the end of the exchange, a little off the mark, and from Vietnam on a helicopter can set one down on a landing zone (Landing by air).
  • The enemy commander resupplies a unit that is out, or low with no enemy in its range, when a source is in reach. Attacking, a unit out of ammunition with none in reach falls back toward its edge; holding, it stays and fights hand to hand.

Heroes

A team's characters go with units as heroes: in the front rank, shooting with it, or behind it. A hero in the front makes 3 times a ranker's attempts with his own attack, and blows on his unit's front fall on him 2 times as often as on a ranker there. His wounds use the full rules, his own Blood and his own stop check. Two front-rank heroes in contact fight each other: 3 attempts each an exchange, instead of at the rankers.

Rank. A hero brings his rank from the team builder. Leading his unit and up, each rank step above the lowest adds 3 to its morale (at most 12). An officer (his rank pays three times a private's or more) draws fire: the blows that fall on his unit's heroes fall on him 2 times as often. What a hero does is counted for the roller: his hits tick his weapon skill, two or more enemies put down are a deed, and a Plains man's close-combat downs are coups (3 honours each).

His wounds slow him as in Wounds: an arm hurt stops a two-handed weapon, and a lamed hero halves his unit's move. In a quiet exchange his friends give first aid: the best Leechcraft in the unit, or its medics, else his comrades at 60%. A lamed or down hero can be carried back by 2 of his unit's men, or left behind. A wounded hero who can still walk can go back alone. Where he goes depends on whether his side has an aid post:

  • With an aid post (the GM places one for each side), the party crosses the map 3 hexes an exchange on open ground by the cheapest way (round water, walls and the enemy, slower through woods), and shells can catch it on the way. At the post he gets first aid every exchange at 75%, and his wounds come off the death clock. An enemy who reaches the post takes or kills the men there. On its side's move the GM can move the post; the men there go with it, and it gives no first aid that exchange.
  • With none, he is carried off the map at once, and the bearers return after 3 exchanges.

A hero left behind lies on his unit's hex. A unit of his side that stands there picks him up; an enemy unit takes him prisoner or kills him, by the war's custom of quarter. When the battle ends, a hero still lying out there is found if his side holds the field; if not, quarter decides.

The retinue: at Towton

On the field map the retinue's followers fight as units: its archers in open order, its spearmen in close order. William of Ely goes with the spearmen in the front rank; Gilbert Cooper shoots with the archers, at his own 55% rather than the unit's quality, and makes 3 times as many aimed shots as one of them. When the billmen close, blows on the archers' front can find him, and a wound there is his own: rolled in full, bled on his own 20 Blood, and carried back to the roller when the battle is over.

The enemy commander

The GM can hand one side to a scripted enemy commander, attacking or holding. At the start of that side's move it orders each unit. It knows only the enemies its units can see (or saw in the last 3 exchanges, where they were then; what a unit sees from where it has just moved, the units ordered after it know); green units go for the nearest, better ones for an enemy that is hurt, shaken or dangerous to them. It closes, takes cover, shoots from range or charges with the odds its quality wants (counting the steady friends touching it, who go in with it), and green units sometimes hesitate. With no enemy in sight, a unit holds; attacking with no objective, it goes forward along its facing to find one. A unit with no room to move facing its goal (or a turn too dear) moves facing as near its goal as it can.

  • Storming works. Attacking, infantry with muskets, rifle-muskets, breech-loaders, or modern rifles and sub-machine guns do not stop to trade fire with an enemy behind works (a parapet, trench or bank), dug in, or in buildings or rubble: they close without seeking cover, firing as they go, and charge it, with the same odds. Flintlock riflemen, archers and machine guns still fight by fire. Modern infantry storm in bounds: a unit that took fire in the last exchange goes to ground and fires this move, and goes on once a bound draws no fire, its target is pinned, or it can charge home. A wall or palisade that blocks hand-to-hand fighting stops them at its foot, unless they carry ladders: then they go up it (see works). Breaching it is the GM's order.

  • Routes. A battlefield can send a unit on a route round a flank, as its account tells: the commander moves it from waypoint to waypoint, turning aside only for an enemy in contact or across its way, then orders it as any other.

  • Orders from the accounts. On the battlefields, units that the sources say held their ground fight where they stand rather than fall back, and units the sources say withdrew on orders fall back at the minute the accounts give, to a place or off the field.
  • Narrowing. Attacking, a formed unit that the ground keeps from closing on its target closes in its front, a quarter at a time and deeper, until it can move nearer, but never to less than half the front it started with.
  • Pursuit. Its horse ride down a broken enemy within a charge when no standing enemy is as near, and its foot go after one within their move that is nearer than any standing enemy. Veterans rally back to the fight after a couple of moves if the enemy still stands near.
  • Shooters give way. Attacking, archers, crossbowmen and skirmishers in open order step aside when they stand in the way of their own formed men behind them, and the formed men go on.
  • In range means the weapon reaches, the light lets it see, and nothing blocks the line from where it would stand.
  • Tanks. A unit with a main gun counts the target in range where the gun reaches and it can see; a vehicle with one prefers a spot where the target can neither reach it nor see it.
  • Reserve. Regulars and veterans hold back their rearmost units (not one on a route, nor tanks and other vehicles with a main gun), and commit one when a unit of theirs breaks or the enemy comes close; veterans also commit to exploit an enemy rout. Attacking, they also commit one when the attack has stalled: five moves without putting down any real share of the enemy or getting nearer. A unit committed because one broke goes to plug the gap where it stood. The GM can mark reserves instead.
  • Digging in. Its foot units with modern weapons dig in where they stand when it is safe (not under fire, no enemy it knows of in their range): at the objective, holding with no objective, and in reserve while they wait.
  • Objective. The GM can mark a hex as its objective. Attacking, its units advance on it when they have nothing better to do and hold it once there (within 1 hex); holding, units more than 3 hexes from it fall back to it. Enemies near it make better targets. The log says who holds it after each exchange. Most battlefields mark the place their battle was fought for, a hill, a bridge, an outpost, as theirs, taking in the whole position (a ring of trenches counts as the hill). The GM can also mark a second objective. Attacking, once it holds the first, the units on it stay and the rest go on to the second (and back to the first if the enemy retakes it); holding, once the enemy holds the first, its units fall back to the second.
  • Minefields. It steers round minefields it knows of. Its sappers, attacking, lift a lane through known enemy mines in the row ahead when those mines lie on the way to their target or the objective, closing up to the belt first and working through it row by row. Holding, or at the objective, with no enemy it knows of within 8 hexes, they lay mines in the row ahead: mixed if the enemy it knows of has vehicles, otherwise anti-personnel.
  • Guns. It turns its guns to face the enemy and calls its off-map batteries and its aircraft (when they can fly; a strafing run or napalm strip along a wide enemy front) on what it sees, first what its forward air controllers see, and closer to its own men there. A controller with nothing to do and no target in its sight moves up to where it sees one (attacking only), up to 3 moves away, a move at a time, preferring a spot out of the enemy's reach; not while it has a fight of its own (an enemy touching it or in its own reach, pinned, or men lost the exchange before). Attacking, one battery lays a creeping barrage ahead of a unit closing on the enemy. Its batteries under counter-battery fire displace (a placed one moves its place 30 hexes along its map edge, away from the battery firing). In the dark it first has one battery fire illumination over the enemy it has lost sight of nearest its men, where it was last seen. Attacking, guns with no enemy in reach go forward: a battery limbers, moves and unlimbers once an enemy is in reach; anti-tank guns hook up to an empty tractor beside them (an empty tractor drives over to fetch them), are towed, and are unhooked in reach. They stop in reach but no nearer than 2 hexes. Holding, its guns unlimber or unhook where they stand. Attacking, its foot units get aboard empty carriers beside them while no known enemy is in reach, and get down once one is (or at the objective). Attacking or holding, guns an enemy could reach at a charge, with no steady friend on the line between, limber or hook up and pull back as far as they can from it. Attacking, it first has one battery smoke an enemy that is shooting at men who cannot reply (not in the dark, or in a gale). Then one battery fires counter-battery on a located enemy battery it can reach: the one with the best counter % on the one with the most guns still served.

Undo its orders puts the move back for the GM to make by hand.

Both sides. Each side has its own choice: moved by the GM, or the commander attacking or holding. With the commander on both sides the GM only watches: Next steps a move at a time, and Run plays on until the GM presses Stop or the run ends itself. It ends when a side has no unit left standing and none still to come, when an attacking side has taken the objective and held it 5 exchanges running with no enemy standing within 109 yards (100 m) of it and none still to come (but not before the battlefield's last phase has begun), or after 60 exchanges (on a battlefield with phases, 30 past the last phase's start, if later, but never more than 1200); then the battle ends, as with End the battle. On a battlefield the side its objective names attacks and the other holds, or the armies fight as the battlefield says they did (the choice marked as fought); on open ground both attack. The GM can take either side back at any time.

The narrative. Under the map, the page tells the battle's turning points as they happen: a phase beginning (and who comes on), units breaking or fleeing, a reserve committed, the objective taken or lost, and the end with each side's losses. With an API key of the player's own, a language model retells each one in a short passage of at most 70 words, in a voice for the war (a chronicle, a dispatch, a war diary or a situation report), or one the GM picks for the battle (any of those, a soldier's account or a plain summary). It is told to use only the facts the game gives it and to write original prose; the plain line stays under each passage. The rules never depend on it.

After the battle

End the battle stops it. The page then sets the two sides' results side by side, and says who holds the field and the objective. Then:

  1. The field. A side with no unit still standing has lost the field: the men it had down there are left behind.
  2. The pursuit. If the other side still has units standing, the beaten side loses more as it flees, as a share of its killed and left on the field (each share rolled between its figures):
Wars Killed in the pursuit Taken prisoner
Crusades, Visby 1361, Wars of the Roses 1-3 times none
Thirty Years' War, American Revolution, Napoleonic Wars, War of 1812, Crimean War 0.25-0.5 times 0.25-0.5 times
American Civil War, American Indian Wars, WWI, WWII, Korea, Vietnam, Late 20th century, Iraq & Afghanistan 0.2-0.5 times 0.5-1.5 times

The victor's fresh horse makes it 1.5 times, and no horse half (before 1850); the dark, half; a river or marsh at the beaten side's back, twice. Most of a beaten medieval army's dead fell in the pursuit; by the 20th century the pursuit takes prisoners. 2. The death clock. A wound that kills in minutes kills before help comes, unless he is bound in time (10%). One that kills in hours kills unless his camp can treat it: 40% saved in a camp, 60% in quarters, none with no camp. Medevac does better where a side had it: ambulance wagons (the Civil War and the Indian Wars) save 50%, motor ambulances (the world wars) 65%, and helicopters (Korea on) 85%, and 20% of those dying within minutes. Helicopters need a landing zone on the field and a helicopter of the side not lost, or it is motor ambulances; the GM can untick a side that had none. 3. To camp. The rest are carried to their force's camp and go onto the track, as in Recovery. A battle set up from the travel map sends its dead and wounded back to the forces there.

The march and the camp

Between battles the team marches, camps and sickens. The travel map moves forces across a map of hexes, usually 0.6 mile (1 km) across, on one clock for everyone.

Marching

A force marches at its kind's road speed:

Force Road speed A day on the road
On foot 2.5 mph (4 km/h) 20 miles (32 km)
Mounted 3.7 mph (6 km/h) 30 miles (48 km)
Baggage wagons 1.9 mph (3 km/h) 15 miles (24 km)

Other ground takes longer; a step from one hex to the next costs the average of the two:

Terrain Time against a road
Road ×1
Open ground ×1.5
Farmland ×1.5
Heath ×1.75
Forest ×2.5
Hills ×2
Mountains ×4
Marsh ×3
River cannot enter
Ford ×2
Bridge ×1
Lake or sea cannot enter
Village ×1
Town ×1

The march starts 1 hour after sunrise and stops 1 hour before sunset, up to 8 hours a day: a short winter day is a short march. Mud and snow slow it (next chapter), and a flooded ford cannot be crossed. These speeds are for a small, fit band; a large army's column made less ground a day.

The clock. Every force on a map keeps the same time, and it moves on only when the GM moves it: an hour, to nightfall, or until something happens. Orders say whether a force marches on its route or halts. When forces of different sides come within 1 hex of each other, the clock stops and both halt: the fight can be set up, on the roller's battle map or the field map, or they can be given new orders.

On the road

An army loses men without a battle. Each night every fit man takes his era's chance of deserting, of falling out and being lost to the force, and of being injured (a fall, a kick, an accident: he joins the sick and wounded), and every man of a mounted force or a wagon train of losing his horse. The chances depend on what the force did that day: in camp they are small (Valley Forge lost 3 men in 10,000 a day to desertion); on the march larger; and withdrawing far larger (the retreat to Corunna lost 1 in 100 a day, the British retreat from Mons nearly 2). A big force simply loses more men. Then there is a chance of an incident: a d100 on the era's table (foragers set on by peasants, a bridge down, a convoy ambushed, a mine in the road, a checkpoint), some for small parties or wagons only, some costing men or a step of fatigue, each with a hook for the GM. The rates come from the records where they exist and are estimates where they do not; the incidents are estimates. At the GM's choice, named characters take the injury chance too.

A force short of food deserts about fifteen times as fast (the starving camp at Nuremberg in 1632) and straggles five times; one whose pay is in arrears deserts three times as fast. The larger applies, not both. A mounted force keeps its count of horses: lost horses, and the horses its deserters ride off on, come off it, and under half a horse a man it marches at foot pace. A wagon train short of teams slows to three quarters, and under half its teams to half. The GM adds remounts when the force finds them.

Loads

What a man carries depends on his order: fighting order (weapon, ammunition, water), marching order (with his pack) or full kit (with extra rations and the rest). Each era has its own weights, from the records where they exist: about 12 kg in fighting order for a Napoleonic redcoat and 27 kg marching, 27 kg on the Somme in 1916, 43 kg on an approach march in Afghanistan. Armour is added where the era's orders leave it out (a medieval man-at-arms' harness, 12 to 22 kg). His load as a share of his body weight (his era's average man's; less for a woman), against his Strength (×0.8 under 30 up to ×1.3 at 75), falls in a band:

Band Load (share of his weight) March (% of the usual) Dodge Blisters (20 km) Extra fatigue
Unburdened 0–15% 100% −0 0% —
Light 15–30% 95% −10 5% —
Medium 30–45% 85% −20 40% a step every 20 km
Heavy 45–65% 70% −35 50% a step every 12 km
Overloaded 65–90% 50% −50, no run 70% a step every 6 km
Immobile over 90% 25% −75, no run 70% a step every 2 km

On the march a force carries its era's marching order unless the GM changes it. The roads' paces are already those of men in marching order, so a heavier order slows the force (the band's march against the usual band's) and tires it more, and a lighter order is no faster. Each named man who marches takes his band's chance of blistered feet (a minor wound on his track): the full chance for 20 km or more, less for a shorter day, a quarter once his feet have hardened after a week on the road, and none while they are still sore.

What he buys weighs. Each thing bought from the price list adds its weight to his load: a musket about 5 kg, a blanket 2, a canteen 1.7, a mail hauberk 9.3 (from the records where they exist, the rest estimates). Food, a bed, a fare, a service and an animal weigh nothing on him. Taking the purchase back off his ledger takes its weight off too. Coin weighs: about a tenth of a kilo for a hundred medieval pennies, and a fat purse of silver is a load; paper money from the Civil War on next to nothing.

Pack animals and carts. A packhorse, mule or wagon bought from the price list carries kit off him, though never what he fights in (his fighting order and his armour):

Animal or vehicle Carries Fodder or fuel a night Wheels
Packhorse 100 kg 0.25 Days —
Mule 100 kg 0.25 Days —
Camel 150 kg 0.2 Days —
Donkey 50 kg 0.15 Days —
A horse (ridden, with saddlebags) 30 kg 0.25 Days —
Dog travois 27 kg 0.1 Days —
Horse travois 110 kg — —
Cart 1,200 kg 0.5 Days yes
Ox wagon 900 kg 0.1 Days yes
Wagon 1,800 kg 1.5 Days yes
Light vehicle 360 kg 0.3 Days (fuel) yes
Motor car 300 kg 0.3 Days (fuel) yes
Motorcycle 40 kg 0.1 Days (fuel) yes
Bicycle 20 kg — yes

Wheels are slow off the road: a force with a cart, wagon or vehicle among its named men marches at 75% off the road and at 50% of that in mud. Where the army does not feed it and the ground cannot graze it (open country, farmland, heath and hills graze), each animal eats its fodder from its owner's purse every night; a vehicle burns its fuel wherever it is. A man with no money for it sees his animals go short.

In a fight a man's band costs his Dodge (his defence is the better of Parry and Dodge less that), and Overloaded or worse he cannot run. A green man (one term) fights a band heavier under fire. Each era fights in its usual order (the British of the Napoleonic wars with their packs on; most others in fighting order). A side may drop its packs before the fight; if it loses the field, the packs are lost with it, and that night its force has no blankets or rations.

Water, heights and pursuit

Swimming. Each man is a non-swimmer, a basic or a strong swimmer, rolled when he is made from his era's rough shares (most medieval men could not swim; perhaps a third of 1940s soldiers could not; a seaman can). In deep water he rolls each minute: d100 at or under his Endurance and:

Swimming
A non-swimmer / basic / strong -50 / +0 / +20
Load band, Unburdened to Immobile +0 / -10 / -25 / -60 / -90 / -100
Armour, light / medium / heavy +0 / -15 / -30
Current, slow / moderate / fast / spate +0 / -10 / -20 / -30
Something to float on +30

A success holds him, a critical lifts him a step, a failure takes him down one (a fumble two): afloat, struggling, going under, drowning, drowned. He may shed his pack (a minute, a load band lighter); plate cannot be shed in the water. Reaching the bank after drowning, he is near-drowned: two steps of fatigue. Cold water takes his breath the first minute (a Nerve check, −20 below 15 °C, −40 at 5 °C or less: failing, a step down), and after a while his limbs fail: from 10 minutes in icy water, 45 at 10-15 °C, he swims 10 worse for every ten minutes more (the 1-10-1 rule; in 10 °C water half of a group of competent swimmers had failed within an hour).

Fords. Infantry could wade to about 3 ft, cavalry 4 ft, guns 2 ft 4 in. Each ford on the travel map has its own depth and current (fixed by its place, deeper and faster in flood). In water deeper than he wades, every named man is at risk; shallower, only a man with a Heavy load or worse. He makes an Agility check (Ride for a horseman) at the current's difficulty:

Current Speed Agility (Ride) Minutes to the bank His horse drowns
Slow 0–0.5 m/s Easy 1 0%
Moderate 0.5–1.5 m/s Ordinary 2 2%
Fast 1.5–3 m/s Hard 3 10%
Spate over 3 m/s Very hard 4 25%

It is the current, not the depth, that sweeps men away: the 10th Hussars' ford on the Kabul River in 1879 was about 3 ft deep with a current of about 4 m/s, and 46 men drowned with 13 horses. Swept off, he takes the water's cold shock (the week's warmth sets how cold it is; a flood is a row colder), then swims for the bank for the current's minutes; a horseman's horse may drown too. A force may choose to risk a flooded ford (never with wagons or guns), and before the motor age baggage wagons cannot cross a ford deeper than 2 ft 4 in at all: they go round by a bridge or a shallower ford. A map may give a ford its own depth and current, where the record has them.

Climbing. Agility + Fieldcraft ÷ 2, for each 10 m of a rope or ladder (3 m of a free climb): a ladder or slope +20, a knotted rope 0, a wet rope or a rough wall −20, a sheer face −40, less for his load and armour. A failure gains no height; a fumble is a fall. A rope or ladder may give way once on the way (a grapnel pulls out, the defenders push the ladder off). At Pointe du Hoc the Rangers climbed 26-30 m cliffs, the first men up within ten minutes.

Falls. By the height, d100:

Height d100
a stumble (up to 1 m) 1-70 none, 71-95 light, 96-100 moderate
a storey, or thrown from a horse (1-3 m) 1-40 light, 41-85 moderate, 86-98 serious, 99-100 grave
two storeys, or from a galloping horse (3-6 m) 1-15 light, 16-55 moderate, 56-90 serious, 91-98 grave, 99-100 dead
6-12 m 1-20 moderate, 21-55 serious, 56-85 grave, 86-100 dead
12-20 m 1-15 serious, 16-50 grave, 51-100 dead
over 20 m 1-10 grave, 11-100 dead

A deliberate feet-first jump that passes an Agility check, or soft ground, is a row lighter; head first, rock, or a heavy load or armour, a row heavier. A moderate injury is a light crush wound, a serious one serious, a grave one critical, and death a critical wound to the head; where it lands follows how he fell (feet first: mostly legs and lower back; thrown from a horse: arms and head). The dead in one modern study had fallen a median 15 m, the survivors 6 m.

Chases are rounds of about ten seconds, the gap close, near, far, distant or lost. Pursuer and quarry roll Agility against each other (Ride on horseback); the winner moves the gap a step, two on a critical, and a tie goes to the faster (a man is slower the heavier his load). A horseman on open ground gains a step every second round whatever the dice; in cover the man on foot has +20 against him. A man on foot tires a step every three rounds, and a horse galloped more than fifteen is blown. Most of the dead of a beaten army fell in the pursuit, not the fight.

Patrons

A patron is a lord, a colonel, a governor, a band chief or a commanding officer: a man who can do things for his clients and expects service. A man's Standing with each patron is a d100 figure, 30 when he is taken on:

Standing He is
0 a stranger to him
1-25 known to him
26-50 his client
51-75 trusted
76+ his right hand

Asking a favour. d100 at his Standing + his Persuade ÷ 10 (asking well), at the favour's difficulty. Granted, it spends Standing: he expects it repaid (a critical spends nothing). Refused, nothing changes; a fumble offends him (-10).

Favour Difficulty Costs Gives
A word for him: a letter, a recommendation, a meal and a bed Easy 2 Standing the GM's word
His word for the next vacancy Ordinary 10 Standing +20 for the next vacancy
Money: a fee, or pay advanced Ordinary 10 Standing 30 Days
A horse or arms Ordinary 10 Standing 40 Days
Work: a month in his service Ordinary 5 Standing 30 Days, 30 days served
A place for his kin Hard 15 Standing the GM's word
A commission: a free vacancy, or the loan of its price Hard 20 Standing +20 for the next vacancy
His ransom paid Hard 20 Standing his ransom
Spared a punishment or a debt Hard 15 Standing the GM's word
Saved from the gallows or a court-martial Very hard 30 Standing the GM's word

His word for a vacancy adds 20 to the man's Command when it is next rolled. Two clients who want the one favour or the one vacancy roll their Standing against each other.

What moves Standing:

Event Standing
A deed he noticed +1d10
A season in his service +2
A gift or his share of the loot +1 for each 5 Days
Horses given away (the Plains nations) +4 a horse
Refused his order or his call -10
Failed on his errand -5
Caught looting or disgraced -5
Changed sides Standing 0, and the patron is his enemy

The patron's fate. At End of season each client gains 2 for the season served, then the patron rolls d100 on his era's line: he may die (his heir takes his clients on at half Standing), fall from favour (each client rolls d100: at or under his Standing he shares the fall, losing his Standing and a rank, or worse at the GM's word; otherwise he gets clear with half), change sides (each client follows, keeping his Standing, or stays and loses it) or go (sold out, disbanded, posted or rotated home: each client may take half his Standing to a new patron).

Era d100
Medieval (c.1250-1460) 3% dies, 2% falls from favour, 1% changes sides
Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) 4% dies, 2% falls from favour, 3% changes sides, 4% disbands his regiment
Horse and musket (1775-1815) 3% dies, 1% falls from favour, 4% sells out or is posted
Crimean War (1854-1856) 5% dies, 1% falls from favour, 3% sells out or goes home
Civil War and frontier (1861-1876) 4% dies, 6% is dismissed by the examining board or resigns, 4% is promoted away
Plains nations (1860-1877) 3% dies, 3% loses his following
First World War (1914-1918) 6% dies, 2% is sent home (stellenbosched), 10% is posted away
Second World War (1939-1945) 4% dies, 2% is relieved, 10% is posted away
Korean War (1950-1953) 3% dies, 2% is relieved, 20% rotates home
Vietnam War (1965-1973) 3% dies, 2% is relieved, 40% ends his six months in command
The Falklands to Afghanistan (1982-2014) 2% dies, 2% is relieved, 25% is posted away

Of Hastings' sixty-seven indentures only two paid a fee: the rest rested on his promise of good lordship. After Wallenstein's murder in 1634 seven generals who had signed for him were demoted and imprisoned, and the men who betrayed him took the estates. Among the Lakota, generosity counted for more than possession: horses given away raise a man's Standing as they raise his honours.

Prisoners

A man taken prisoner is not simply lost. The GM picks his captors' situation from his era's list, and any circumstances: a garrison stormed after refusing terms (+20), captors who had just lost heavily (+15), one they gave no quarter (+30), a formal surrender (−25), a man visibly worth a ransom (−20, where ransom was the custom), taken wounded (+5). Roll d100 less those figures: at or under the first figure below he is killed out of hand, at or under the second stripped and robbed (his purse is taken), and otherwise held with his things.

Each season (3 months) he is held: first a d100 for release (an exchange, parole, the war's end); if not, an escape if he tries (Stealth, with the camp's figure, to get out, then Fieldcraft to get home; retaken, he may be killed for it, and every recapture makes his captivity harsher); then the death check at his captors' rate (doubled in a hard winter, halved for an officer kept apart, a quarter for an officer on parole). Each season adds Strain, two in a harsh camp (3% a season or worse), where he also loses a point of Endurance. Released, ransomed or escaped, he rejoins the team.

Era Captors Killed at or under Stripped at or under Released a season Dies a season Also

1914-18 Russians in German or Austro-Hungarian hands 8 40 2% 1% —
1914-18 Serbs in Austro-Hungarian, Bulgarian or German hands 8 40 1% 3% —
1914-18 Germans or Austro-Hungarians in Russian hands 8 40 1% 2% —
