1914-18 Romanians in Bulgarian hands 8 40 1% 2% —
1914-18 Austro-Hungarians in Serbian hands (the typhus, the retreat) 8 40 1% 6% —
1939-45 Western Allies and Germans, either way 5 40 2% 0.4% —
1939-45 An officers' camp or Colditz 5 40 2% 0.3% —
1939-45 Soviet prisoners of the Germans, 1941-42 25 75 0% 30% —
1939-45 The Eastern Front, 1942-45, either way 25 75 0% 5% —
1939-45 Allied prisoners of the Japanese 25 70 0% 2.2% —
Korea Taken in the winter of 1950-51 15 60 0% 25% (then 2%) —
Korea Taken after mid-1951 5 40 0% 1% —
Vietnam Held in the North 5 60 1% 0.7% —
1982-2014 The Falklands or the Gulf 1 20 95% 0% —
1982-2014 Chechnya 20 70 15% 8% ransom

Ransom (medieval, Thirty Years' War officers, Chechnya): about a year of his pay and his keep for a medieval man, a month's pay for each step of rank for an officer of the Thirty Years' War, and what a family could raise in Chechnya; paid from his purse or the leader's. Parole: an officer of 1700 to 1865 may give his word, and is held freer and safer; escaping then breaks it. Under the Dix-Hill cartel of 1862 men were paroled within ten days and exchanged by rank (a corporal or sergeant 2 privates, a lieutenant 4, a captain 6, a colonel 15, a general 60); a paroled man may not fight until he is exchanged. Service: in the Thirty Years' War and under Napoleon a captured man of the ranks might join his captors' regiment, and desert back when he could (at Stadtlohn in 1623 a thousand of four thousand prisoners joined Tilly, and most deserted).

The team's own captives. A man the team takes is kept on its list. Each End of season each captive eats 0.5 Days a day from the leader's purse, and each not on parole tries to escape: his Stealth 50 against the team's best Watch, 10 worse for each captive more than the team's own number. He may be ransomed (his people pay the leader his era's ransom, an officer's at 3 times a soldier's pay), exchanged for one of the team held, put on parole (he gives his word, does not try to escape, and keeps himself), or let go. Questioning him is words across tongues with the team's best speaker of his tongue, or its interpreter: a critical, he tells all he knows; a success, something useful; a failure, little; a fumble, a wrong answer believed. A captive's ransom is shared as loot is: the medieval third goes to the leader's lord (a gift to a patron who takes thirds), the Swedish hospitals take their tenth. When the team's side chases a beaten enemy on the field map, the prisoners taken in the pursuit are offered to the team, as many as the GM will put in its charge. (A postwar report credited the US Army's German-speaking interrogators, the Ritchie Boys, with nearly 60% of the credible intelligence gathered in Europe.)

By night

A force may march on by night, up to 4 hours after the day's marching hours, at about two-thirds of the pace (a 1979 US Army study timed night navigation about 40% slower). Its guide, the best Fieldcraft among its named men, rolls once a night to keep the way: Ordinary on a road, Hard off it. Failing, the night's march goes slower still; on a fumble the column spends 2 hours on the wrong road, as the guides did at Stormberg in 1899, wandering the veld until dawn. A night march of 2 hours or more costs a step more fatigue.

Boots and clothing

Each named man's boots wear with every day he marches, faster on wet or muddy ground, and his clothing and blankets with every day, twice as fast on a hard night. Lives in days:

Era Boots (marching days) Clothing (days)
Civil War and frontier 45 120
Crimean War 60 180
Horse and musket 60 365
Korean War 105 90
Medieval 60 180
The Falklands to Afghanistan 120 120
Plains nations 4 90
Thirty Years' War 60 180
Vietnam War 60 60
First World War 51 79
Second World War 105 90

Worn boots raise his chance of blistered feet (half again; worn out, three times); worn clothing makes his nights a step colder and wetter (worn out, two), for his recovery and for frostbite. On a day his force does not march, its best Craft mends the most worn boots or clothing among its named men (Mend kit: a success takes half the wear off, a fumble ruins them). He may buy new from the price list (boots, shoes, a coat, a blanket), and a force its army feeds is issued new at its depot. In October 1862 the 48th North Carolina returned 51 of its 619 men barefoot and 194 more nearly so; at Valley Forge 2,898 men were unfit for duty, "barefoot and otherwise naked".

Supplies

A force carries what it needs between fights: ammunition (a share of its full loads), rations (days a man carries), water (litres a man) and medical stores:

Era Rations carried (days) Water carried (L a man)
Civil War and frontier 3 1.4
Crimean War 3 1.1
Horse and musket 4 1.4
Korean War 3 0.95
Medieval 4 1
The Falklands to Afghanistan 3 3
Plains nations 3 1
Thirty Years' War 3 1
Vietnam War 3 3
First World War 2 1.1
Second World War 2 0.95

Rations. A day its army does not feed it, and it has not foraged or hunted its food, it eats a day's rations; with none left it goes hungry (desertion and straggling run higher, and its named men have a hard night). A Union quartermaster reckoned that of eight days issued, hardly five could be counted on. Water. By a river, lake, ford, marsh, bridge, village or town, or in rain, it fills up; elsewhere each man needs 2 L on a cool day, 3 L on a warm one, 5 L in heat and 8 L in great heat; short of it, the force is thirsty: a step more fatigue and a hard night. Medical stores serve 10 wounded or sick for each hundred men; each new wounded man draws one and each sick man a seventh a day; with none left its sick and wounded are cared for a step worse in camp. Ammunition goes into a battle on the field map as its share of a load, and what is left comes back.

It refills everything at its army's depot (where it started on the map, or a place marked a depot of its side, flagged ⚑ on the map: Harfleur and Calais for Henry V, Balaklava and Kamiesh before Sevastopol, Hagaru-ri and Koto-ri at Chosin), draws from its baggage train in the same hex (the train carries 10 days' rations, 2 loads of ammunition and 2 fills of medical stores for 1,000 men, and a larger force takes more of it), and where its army does not feed it its named men may buy a day's rations for every man in a village or town at their army's keep.

Camps

At the end of the march a force makes camp:

Camp What it is Needs Surprise Rest
Bivouac Sleep where you stop. Nothing built and no proper watch. — +20 poor
Watched camp A cleared site with fires, the baggage drawn up and a sentry roster. — 0 fair
Staked camp A watched camp ringed with sharpened stakes, like archers' stakes set against horse. tools −10 fair
Fortified camp Ditch, bank and palisade all round, with a gate. tools −20 good
Quartered Billeted in the houses of a village or town. village, town 0 good

Digging takes the work of the camp's ditches, banks, palisades and stakes, laid out as the battle map would lay them, divided among the men (75% of them work at once; the rest guard and cook). Camp work can use what is left of the marching day and then 4 evening hours; beyond that it runs on into the next day.

Surprise. When a fight is set up from the travel map, the defenders may be caught unawares: 30%, plus the camp's figure above (10 more with no camp at all), +20 in the dark, +20 in fog, plus the attackers' best Stealth ÷ 5, less the defenders' best Watch ÷ 5, and never under 5% or over 95%. Surprised men cannot attack or move in the first round.

Skills on the march

The best named man in the force rolls; a skill used well is ticked.

Billets. A force its army does not feed must find its own quarters in a village or town: his Persuade (no better than his tongue there). Fail, and no one will take them in. Quartered, its named men pay no bed; in the Thirty Years' War the host fed them too (a Leipzig ordinance of 1639: soup, a vegetable, cheese, bread and beer). A force its army feeds is billeted by authority.

Hunting for the pot. In open country, heath, forest, hills or marsh, Fieldcraft at nightfall: a deer feeds 5 men for a day (Lewis and Clark's party ate 9 lb of meat a man), a buffalo 40 where they ran; a critical, twice that. Meat for the whole force feeds it however short of food, and it is fresh.

Finding the way. Off the road, or in fog, snow, a storm or a sandstorm, the guide's Fieldcraft once a day (Hard in fog, a blizzard or a sandstorm). Fail, and the day's march goes 1.4 times as long (night navigation ran about 40% slower in a 1979 US Army study); fumble, and an hour is lost going the wrong way first.

Finding work

Between fights a man may hire himself out. Where the team is (a town, city, village, camp, the road, the frontier or at sea) decides which jobs are on offer; he may take any of them that his career allows and his skill reaches (the least skill to be hired). Pay is in Days for each day worked, or a sum for the whole contract, a horse or a body.

A job is worked in terms: a day, a week (7 days), a month (30 days) or a contract of so many days. Each term he makes one check on the job's skill. At or under it, he is paid in full; over it, 50% of the pay; 96 or more and over, a fumble, and nothing. A job with no skill pays in full.

A job with a risk takes one d100 a term as well: at or under the risk, trouble. The GM uses the job's hook, or rolls a d10 on the era's trouble table. Jobs marked † are against the law, and their trouble is the law's.

Keep. A soldier with his army is fed by it. A man who is not (off on his own, on leave, or working for someone else) pays his keep from his purse each day: a day's food (3d (½ Day) for an English archer), and a bed (1½d (¼ Day)) where there is one to be had: in a town, city or village, or at an inn on the road (on the travel map, a night in a village or town out of camp). A job marked (fed) feeds him while he works: his army's own service, or wages paid with board. A day he cannot pay for his food he goes hungry: it counts as a day without fresh food, and tires him a step. A night he cannot pay for a bed he sleeps rough. The medieval jobs:

Job Skill Pay Term Where Who Risk
Ransom broker Persuade 50 3 Days a day 30-90 days town, frontier, road clerk or priest, merchant, man-at-arms, mercenary 20%
Free-company routier Blade 45 2 Days a day a month camp, frontier, road mercenary, man-at-arms, crossbowman, archer, mounted sergeant 40%

Hired scribe Letters 40 1 Day a day a week town, city, camp anyone none
Indentured archer Bow 45 1 Day a day 90-365 days camp, frontier archer, forester or huntsman 30%
Merchant's guard Watch 40 1 Day a day 7-21 days road anyone 20%

Debt collector Brawl 35 ¾ Day a day a week town, city anyone 15%
Harvest hand Fieldcraft 0 ¾ Day a day a week village anyone none
Siege miner Craft 30 ¾ Day a day a week camp anyone 35%
Cog crew (fed) Seamanship 30 ½ Day a day 21-42 days sea, town anyone 20%
Minstrel Persuade 30 ½ Day a day a day town, city, village, camp anyone 5%
Sick-nurse (fed) Leechcraft 30 ½ Day a day a week town, city, camp anyone 10%
Tournament servitor (fed) Ride 30 ½ Day a day 3-7 days town, city anyone 15%
Carter (fed) Ride 20 ¼ Day a day a month village, road anyone 5%
Hired watchman Watch 0 ¼ Day a day a week town, city anyone 10%
Ostler or tapster (fed) Persuade 0 ¼ Day a day a month town, city, road anyone 5%
Battlefield stripper † Stealth 0 2 Days a day a day camp, frontier anyone 35%
Wool smuggler † Seamanship 30 2 Days a day 2-5 days sea, village anyone 30%

Poacher † Stealth 30 ½ Day a day a week village, frontier anyone 25%
d10 Trouble
1 Hurt at the work: a fall, a kick or a blade. A light wound, and the rest of the term's pay is lost.
2 The employer won't pay, pays short or pays in clipped coin: half, unless he can be made to pay.
3 Taken before the justices for wages above the statute, or for vagrancy: fined a week's pay.
4 A brawl with rival workers, soldiers or locals: a Brawl check or a wound, and a grudge either way.
5 Fever, flux or plague in the lodging: a recovery check, or a week sick.
6 Robbed on the road or in bed: the term's earnings are gone.
7 Pressed into a lord's array or onto a king's ship, willing or not.
8 Falsely accused of theft or worse: find a witness, flee, or face the court.
9 Raiders, enemy soldiers or pirates fall on the place: a fight with a real enemy.
10 He saw something he should not have: a powerful man wants his silence, and may buy it or end it.

The other 10 eras' jobs are in the printed tables and the team builder.

Rank, pay and loot

Rank. Each era has its ladder of ranks; a man starts at the bottom unless his career puts him higher (a sergeant, an officer). The medieval ladder, from the Calais muster of 1346 (in truth a man's place was his contract, and rises like an archer's to man-at-arms were rare):

Rank Pay (× a soldier's) Least years in the rank below Command check
Soldier 1 — —
Vintenar 2 2 Ordinary
Man-at-arms 4 10 Very hard
Knight 8 4 Very hard, only after a deed

Promotion. A rank falls vacant when a man of it is lost, or when the GM opens one for the wider company's losses. At the end of a season each vacancy is offered to the team's men one rank below who have served its years in that rank (or did a deed in battle, which waives the time and adds +20) and, where the army demanded it, can read and write (Letters 20 or more: British sergeants in the Napoleonic wars, officers in the Civil War). The most senior rolls Command first, at the rank's difficulty; the first to succeed is promoted, and his old rank falls vacant in turn. A man can be reduced to a lower rank at the GM's word. The roller suggests a deed for a man who put down two or more enemies, or their leader, in a fight; the GM confirms it.

Buying a commission. In the British army of 1700 to 1871, most officers bought their rank. A British officer (or a man about to become one) may buy the next rank when it falls vacant, at the regulation price (£450 for an ensign, £1,800 for a captain of the line), less the price of the commission he already holds; the unofficial price ran half again to double, which the GM may ask. On leaving the army he may sell out and take his commission's price with him. Free commissions still came by death in action and to sergeants promoted from the ranks (the ordinary roll above).

Pay. Each day his force is fed by its army, a man earns his rank's pay, less what the army stopped for his rations and necessaries, paid into his purse at the end of the season. Days when his force's pay is in arrears are owed instead, until the GM says the arrears are paid. Horsemen and surgeons may draw more; a sutler draws nothing. Nurses and auxiliaries draw their own army's rates: a Union nurse 40 cents a day and a ration, a Confederate one up to $25 a month (more than twice a private's), a QAIMNS nurse of 1914 £30 to £35 a year, the ATS two-thirds of a private's pay, and from 1947 an American army nurse a second lieutenant's; a vivandière, a camp woman and a soldier's wife draw none.

Loot. After a won fight (the roller sees when one side alone is still standing, or the GM names the winner, or the field map says who held the field), the field: each man rolls d100 (a stormed town's sack adds 15, though only a 100 is a windfall):

d100 He finds Worth (Days)
1–35 nothing worth the carrying —
36–60 food, tobacco, a blanket 1–3
61–80 boots, a good coat, a knife 3–8
81–92 a purse or a watch 10–30
93–99 silver, a fine weapon 30–90
100 a windfall: jewels, a paymaster's chest 200–1000

His era takes its share (the medieval captain a third, the Swedish hospitals a tenth). The medieval third went to his lord: given to a patron who takes thirds, it is a gift and raises his Standing. Where plunder is forbidden (the Crimea's provost, the Lieber Code of 1863, the Hague rules of 1907), or past what a man may keep as a trophy, the provost rolls his Watch against the man's Stealth: if the provost wins, the loot is taken from him, and on the provost's critical or the man's fumble the era's punishment follows (hanging, flogging, a court-martial). In the eras of prize money each man draws his rank's shares (at Waterloo, a private one share of about 51 days' pay, a captain 35). A medieval or Thirty Years' War prisoner may be ransomed (with leave).

Honours. The Plains nations had no ranks and no pay. A man's honours come from coups counted (the first to strike counts most: the roller counts it when his blow lands in close combat) and horses taken from an enemy camp; his horses are his wealth, and giving them away turns wealth into standing.

Sickness

Before antibiotics, disease emptied armies faster than battle. Once a week every well man may catch what the camp breeds, at a chance set by its hygiene (a bivouac is poor, quarters good, other camps fair), by staying four weeks or more in one place, by the ground (marsh, a town) and by the week's weather:

Disease Caught from Shows after Deaths per case (records)
Bloody flux Dirty water or food, latrines too near the water 1–3 days 2.6%
Camp fever (typhus) Lice in crowded, unwashed camps 7–14 days 40%
Typhoid Dirty water or food, often from a carrier in camp 7–21 days 36%
Ague (malaria) Mosquitoes in marshes and low wetlands 7–28 days 0.8%
Plague Flea bites; worst in sieges and towns full of rats 2–6 days 45%

A case climbs to its peak after it shows, then gets better or worse each night on the track of Recovery, with rest, a camp and shelter helping, and marching, cold wet nights and filth hurting. Survivors of typhus and plague cannot catch it again; ague comes back in marsh country.

  • What it costs. Men at serious or worse cannot dig, fight or march on their own; at grave or worse they are carried on litters. A force carrying litters marches at 90%, or 50% with fewer than 2 fit men a litter.
  • Scurvy. After 6 weeks without fresh food (fruit, greens, fresh meat, onions), each week every well man may fall ill: 10% the first week, 10 more each week after, against his Endurance. Fresh food heals it 2 steps a week. A scurvied man's old wounds open again.
  • Frostbite. On a night of 5 °F (-15 °C) or colder, men without enough shelter may be frostbitten, a sickness on the same track.

The retinue: on the road

The retinue marches north on foot: 20 miles (32 km) a day on the road when the days are long, less in March, when Towton was fought, and less again in the snow that fell that day. It makes a watched camp each night, with a sentry roster and fires; no tools are needed. In a fair camp, moving on every day, the flux is the only real danger; were it to sit in a filthy siege camp for a month, typhus would come for it.

For the GM

The travel map counts all of this for whole forces, and runs each named character's own case with his own Endurance when you put him With a force from the roller. Your job is the choices: how hard to march, where to camp, whether to wait for the sick.

Weather, light and works

The day's weather

Each day on the travel map rolls its weather from the climate's figures for the month: its highs and lows, its days of rain and fog, its winds. Wet and dry spells last, and a warm or cold spell carries over. Rain falls as snow when the day's high is 36 °F (2 °C) or less. The GM can roll again or set any of it by hand. A sandstorm is never rolled: a battlefield names it (73 Easting, 1991) or the GM sets it.

Mud and snow build up and wear off day by day. On the travel map they slow the going; on the battle map, mud or snow at level 2 or more costs one more hex of movement every hex. Heavy rain or a storm floods the fords for 2 days, counting that day.

Weather in a fight

Weather affects missiles, never close combat:

Weather Can aim to Bows and crossbows
Fair no limit —
Overcast no limit —
Fog 55 yards (50 m) —
Rain 328 yards (300 m) −10%
Heavy rain 164 yards (150 m) −20%
Storm 109 yards (100 m) −20%
Snow 164 yards (150 m) −10%
Heavy snow 87 yards (80 m) −10%
Blizzard 33 yards (30 m) −20%
Sandstorm 437 yards (400 m) —
Wind Bows, slings, thrown Firearms Range bands with or into it
Calm or light air — — —
Breeze — — ±10%
Strong wind −10% — ±20%
Gale −20% −10% ±30%

Shooting with the wind lengthens the range bands of bows, crossbows, slings and thrown weapons; shooting into it shortens them, and rain or snow in a shooter's face halves how far he can see to aim. In the wet, a firearm can misfire, losing the shot:

Ignition Rain or snow Heavy rain, storm, blizzard
Match 30% 60%
Wheel 15% 30%
Flint 15% 30%
Percussion 5% 10%
Cartridge — —

Fatigue

A hard march, heat or cold, deep going, a bad night and hand-to-hand fighting tire a character a step at a time; a good night's rest takes it back. On the field map whole units tire the same way, from hand-to-hand fighting and deep going (an exchange):

Fatigue Attack and defence Marching speed
Fresh — 100%
Tired −5% 100%
Weary −10% 90%
Exhausted −20% 75%
Spent −30% 0%

Light

In the dark no one can see to aim, or to call fire, past the light's reach, and aimed fire is harder. A battlefield can change the light as its battle goes on, at sunset or dawn. A flare or an illumination round lights its hexes as by day for a few exchanges, and night-vision devices of the later wars see further:

Light Can see to aim Aimed fire
Daylight no limit —
Dusk or dawn 219 yards (200 m) −5%
Moonlit night 109 yards (100 m) −10%
Dark night 55 yards (50 m) −20%

Works

Camps and battlefields have works: along a hex's sides (ditches, banks, palisades, gates, walls) or in a hex (stakes, felled trees, wagons, trenches, bunkers):

Work Cover Crossing Blocks close combat
Ditch — +2 movement —
Earth bank −20% +1 movement —
Palisade −40% cannot be crossed (breach it) yes
Gate −40% free yes
Stone wall −50% cannot be crossed (breach it) yes
Stakes — +1 movement —
Abatis −20% +2 movement —
Pavise −20% free —
Wagon −40% cannot be crossed (breach it) —
Barbed wire — +3 movement —
Bunker −50% +1 movement —
Trench −40% +1 movement —
Downed helicopter −30% +2 movement —

A palisade, wall, barred gate or wagon must be breached to get through: men hack at it instead of fighting, until it is down. Across a palisade, wall or barred gate only reach-2 weapons strike, from the front rank, and striking up a bank or ditch costs its height. Horses cannot charge into stakes or felled trees.

On the field map, men on foot the GM marks with ladders can escalade a palisade, wall or barred gate instead: a few men a hex fight from the ladders at −20%, the defenders strike back at them, and once the far side is clear the unit can climb over at a cost of 4 hexes of movement.

For the GM

Weather is the cheapest way to change a fight. Rain on the morning of a battle takes the archers' edge away and spoils matchlocks; fog lets the attackers close unseen; a gale at the archers' backs carries their arrows nearly a third further. Roll it, then let the players decide whether to fight in it.

Other wars

Everything so far has used the medieval tables. The same rules carry a team through 10 more eras, from the Thirty Years' War to Afghanistan. Each era has its own skills, origins, careers, events, armies, teams, followers and jobs. Pick one with Era in the team builder.

The eras

Era Armies Fighting skills Careers A term
Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) The Swedish army (Swedes, Finns, Scots and Germans), The Imperial army and the Catholic League Musket, Pistol, Blade, Pike 10 4 years
Horse and musket (1775-1815) The Continental Army (1775-1783), The British Army in America (1775-1783), The British in the Peninsula (1808-1814), The French Empire in Spain (1808-1814), The United States (1812-1815) Musket, Rifle, Pistol, Blade, Bayonet, Gunnery 12 4 years
Crimean War (1854-1856) British, French, Russian Musket, Pistol, Blade, Bayonet, Gunnery 11 4 years
Plains nations (1860-1877) The Lakota (Oglala, Minneconjou and other bands), The Cheyenne and Arapaho Bow, Lance, Club and knife, Gun 7 4 years
Civil War and frontier (1861-1876) The Union (1861-1865), The Confederacy (1861-1865), The US Army on the frontier (1866-1876) Rifle, Pistol, Blade, Bayonet, Gunnery 11 4 years
First World War (1914-1918) The British Empire, France, Germany, The United States (1917-1918), Russian, Serbian, Austro-Hungarian, Bulgarian Rifle, Pistol, Machine gun, Bombing, Gunnery, Bayonet, Trench weapons 12 1 year
Second World War (1939-1945) The United States in Europe, US Marines and Army in the Pacific, The British Commonwealth, Germany, The Soviet Union, Japan Rifle, SMG and pistol, Machine gun, Grenade, Gunnery, Bayonet, Close combat 13 1 year
Korean War (1950-1953) US 1950-51, US 1952-53, Commonwealth, ROK, Chinese, North Korea Rifle, SMG and pistol, Machine gun, Grenade, Gunnery, Bayonet, Close combat 12 1 year
Vietnam War (1965-1973) US Army, US Marines, ANZAC, ARVN, North Vietnam, Viet Cong Rifle, SMG and pistol, Machine gun, Grenade and rocket, Gunnery, Bayonet, Close combat 12 1 year
The Falklands to Afghanistan (1982-2014) UK 1982, Argentina 1982, US 1991, US 1993, Russia 1995, Chechens, US 2003-14, UK 2003-14, Insurgents Rifle, Pistol, Machine gun, Grenade and rocket, Gunnery, Bayonet, Close combat 12 1 year

Brawl, Parry and Dodge carry over to every era, and so do the skills used outside a fight (Leechcraft, Fieldcraft, Watch, Stealth and the rest). Bow, Crossbow, Axe and Sling stay medieval (the Plains nations have their own Bow). Gunnery is the skill of men who serve guns, mortars (and, in the Crimea, of sailors serving ships' guns ashore) and, in Korea, rocket launchers and recoilless rifles. In the Crimea one Musket skill covers both the smoothbore musket and the rifle-musket. From Vietnam on, the RPG is fired with Grenade and rocket.

What changes

  • A term. Before 1914 a career term is 4 years, as in the medieval tables. From the First World War on, a term is 1 year of the war, so a soldier of three terms is about twenty-one.
  • Wound tables. Each army rolls on its own war's wound table, both for old wounds when a character is made and in the roller. Where a war's records have no wounds of some kind, the table borrows the nearest one: the pike is rolled as a long spear, and the frontier's gunshots come from the Civil War table.
  • Armour. It follows the army and the year:
  • pikemen's and cuirassiers' armours in the 1630s;
  • the steel helmet from 1915–16;
  • nylon flak vests in Korea and Vietnam;
  • plate armour in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Many armies wore none. A vest's rating against each threat (fragments, pistol rounds, rifle rounds) decides how many steps it takes off a wound, so a vest that stops a grenade fragment may do nothing against a rifle bullet. The roller and the field map read the same kits. - Kit and weapons come with the career and the army: a Viet Cong RPG gunner carries an RPG, a Second World War tank crewman a submachine gun. - Names are common names of the period and place, put together at random, and are not meant to name anyone. Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese names are written family name first.

Women under arms

Where the records show women serving in a career, the team builder can roll a woman for it at that army's share. A career with its own share (in brackets below) rolls at that instead: the camp women of the Thirty Years' War's baggage train, the French vivandières (four to a battalion from 1793), the British soldiers' wives on the strength (six in a hundred men went overseas, by lot), the nurses from Scutari to Vietnam, the auxiliaries of both world wars (the ATS made up two-thirds of the crews of Britain's mixed heavy anti-aircraft batteries), and the Female Engagement Teams of Iraq and Afghanistan. Women who fought are open where the records show them, chosen rather than rolled: the townswomen who defended Toulouse in 1218 and Dunbar in 1338, Margaret Corbin at her husband's gun and Deborah Sampson in the Continental line, the Lakota and Cheyenne women at the Rosebud and the Little Bighorn, the Russian women's battalions of 1917 (Bochkareva's reached the third German line at Smorgon), Serbia's women sergeants and Flora Sandes, a British nurse who enlisted as a private in the retreat of 1915, and Austria-Hungary's few (Viktoria Savs, disguised as a man with the Standschützen; Olena Stepaniv, an officer of the Ukrainian Sich Riflemen). In every other army a career rolls a man, and the page gives the reason. An army's share is the women among its soldiers as a whole, not just in that career, so treat it as a rough guide. A GM may prefer to choose.

Army Share Careers open to women

For the GM

Pick an era for the fighting you want, not the uniforms. Before the machine gun, battles are decided in the press and the rout, as in the medieval chapters. From 1914 on, men are put down by fire they never see, and what matters is cover, going to ground and the guns. The next chapters cover that.

Guns and fire support

The field map uses the same exchange for every era. What changes after 1865 is the weight of fire, and how men live under it.

Modern infantry

  • Extended order. 3 men to a hex, a few yards apart. Shots at them count half, and they move 8 hexes.
  • Rifles. In a minute a bolt-action rifle fires 10 rounds, a self-loading or assault rifle 15, and a submachine gun or pistol 12. They are rolled as aimed shots at the same rate as a musket's: most rounds are fired at the enemy's line, not at a man.
  • Modern fire puts men down. Against breech-loaders and later weapons, shell and grenades, every serious or critical wound puts a man down, and a light one calls for the stop check (An exchange).
  • Going to ground. On its own move a unit can go to ground in the folds of the ground. Shots at it lose 15% on top of its cover. It cannot move until it gets up, but it still shoots and fights hand to hand.
  • Digging in. A unit with a modern weapon, out of contact, can dig shell scrapes and foxholes: 3 exchanges without moving or firing, and it is dug in where it stands. Dug in, it counts as gone to ground (and hidden, and steadier) while it stays there, but it can get up and move, leaving its holes. In set-up the GM can start units dug in.
  • Hidden men. Men gone to ground, in a trench or a bunker, or in buildings or rubble show little of themselves. Only 10% of the aimed shots at them find a man to aim at (5% of a machine gun's); the rest go at the smoke and the flashes. Dug-in men also hold better: +10 on morale.
  • Machine guns. A machine-gun team serves one gun for every 5 men, and the gun fires while one of its crew is up. It fires 300 rounds a minute, and one in 10 is rolled as an aimed shot.
  • The beaten zone. The cone of fire falls on past its target. The first other unit (friend or foe) within 219 yards (200 m) beyond the target on the line of fire takes 50% as many shots. Woods, rough ground and marsh stop it.
  • Pinned. A unit near a shell burst, or under a machine gun's fire (in its beaten zone too), checks at the end of the exchange: d100 against its Nerve, +10 if gone to ground. On a failure it is pinned for the next exchange: it cannot move, and it shoots at half its rate.

Guns of the black-powder wars

A battery is a unit in battery order, 20 men to a hex. Its men are the crews, 10 to a gun, so as crews fall fewer guns are served.

  • Its fire. Each served gun fires a round an exchange at the nearest enemy in front of it, in sight and with a clear line of fire, out to 1,094 yards (1,000 m) (1,750 yards (1,600 m) for rifled guns). The GM can name another target, split the guns into sections, or choose the shot.
  • Canister. Within 328 yards (300 m) the guns fire canister: 8 chances a round, each likely to hit at short range and less so beyond.
  • Round shot. Beyond that range the guns fire round shot. A ball that strikes a unit ploughs through its ranks, and each man in its path is hit at 40%, so a deep column suffers far more than a line. On firm ground the ball bounds on, and it can strike another unit up to 328 yards (300 m) beyond.
  • Shell. Howitzers fire shell over anything in the way. Its fuse may burst it early, in the air over the men, on the ground, or not at all. Gunners who have found the range cut their fuses better.
  • Wounds. Every man struck by a gun rolls a wound at 80%, with no parry.
  • Rounds. Each gun carries 50 rounds into action. Resupply takes an exchange.
  • Limbering. Changing between limbered and unlimbered takes an exchange. Unlimbered, the guns can only be pushed 2 hexes.
  • Losing the guns. A battery that breaks loses its guns for good.
  • Canister at the charge. Charged in front, a battery gives the first charger one round of canister at point-blank range before the melee.

Fire support

From the First World War on, a side can have batteries off the map: mortars, field guns, heavy howitzers, and tanks or autocannon firing over open sights. Each is a number of tubes with their rounds and crews.

Kind Reach Shells a minute a tube Rounds a tube Lands Scatter Struck % at 0, 1, 2 … hexes
Mortars 2.2 miles (3.6 km) 3 60 this exchange 2 hexes 15, 5, 1
Field guns 6.8 miles (11 km) 2 80 next exchange 4 hexes 20, 8, 3, 1
Heavy howitzers 9.0 miles (14.5 km) 1 40 next exchange 5 hexes 30, 12, 5, 2, 1, 0.5
Tanks (direct fire) in sight 2 60 this exchange none 25, 5
Autocannon (direct fire) in sight 3 300 this exchange none 20
  • Calling fire. On its side's move a battery fires on a hex that one of the side's units can see. That means within the weather's sight and the light's, with no woods or smoke between. It can keep firing each exchange until stopped or out of rounds.
  • Where it lands. Each shell scatters by a d6 for the direction and up to the kind's scatter in hexes.
  • What it does. Every man in the burst is struck at the % for his distance from it, ×0.35 if gone to ground and less his cover. A struck man rolls a wound as one hit by shell fragments at 70%. With quick-play, add up each man's chance (men × their % for each burst) for the average and roll once on the spread chart for the men struck.
  • Tree bursts. Over woods, shells burst in the branches. The woods give no cover, the chance is ×1.5, and going to ground only brings it to ×0.7.
  • Smoke spends the same rounds and wounds no one. No one sees or shoots into, out of or through it, and it drifts downwind:
Wind Exchanges it screens after landing Drifts (hexes an exchange)
Calm or light air 3 —
Breeze 2 1
Strong wind 1 2
Gale none: blown away 2
  • Illumination lights the ground round its aim as by day (see Night and the air). It needs no one to see the hex.
  • A fire plan. A creeping barrage lifts its aim 1 to 3 hexes after 1 to 4 exchanges on each line, ahead of an advance kept to the same timetable. A plan can have up to eight legs, each going on the same way or turning.
  • Counter-battery. A battery that has fired is located. Field guns and heavy howitzers can fire on it with no one needing to see it:
  • each shell lands among its guns at 2% (field guns) or 4% (heavy howitzers), knocking out a tube and striking 2 of its crew;
  • at 3 times that chance, it bursts close by and strikes one man.

Counter-battery wears a battery down over a battle rather than ending it. Displacing silences a battery for an exchange or more and leaves it no longer located. - On the map. A battery can stand on a hex of the map instead. From there it reaches only its range, and an enemy unit next to it overruns it.

Trenches and bunkers

A trench gives the men in it cover and hides them, but they fight hand to hand as usual. A bunker shelters its men from shots and shellfire and from blows: no one strikes them, and they strike no one, but they shoot out of it. A tank's shell bursting on it knocks it out at 8%, a heavy howitzer's at 2%.

To take a bunker, a unit next to it storms it with one of three means, once an exchange for each enemy-held bunker across its front, +20 if the bunker's men are pinned:

Means Knocks the bunker out on d100 Men in its hex struck
Grenades 10 or less 40%, as grenade wounds
Satchel charges 25 or less 60%, as grenade wounds
Flamethrowers 40 or less 70%, burned

A man reached by flame is out of the fight with critical burns, and 40% of them are killed outright. A knocked-out bunker is a hex like any other.

For the GM

Under modern fire the question each exchange is who can see whom. Units in the open in close order are cut down. Spread out and gone to ground, they are hard to hit but are pinned half the time. Let the players find a way to move: smoke, a fire plan, a covered approach, or the dark.

Vehicles

On the field map, in wars with machine guns or later, tanks, infantry fighting vehicles and armoured carriers fight as units, one vehicle to a hex. The unit's men are its crews.

Vehicle Crew Move (hexes) Armour Main gun: reach, rounds, hits (close / mid / full) Carries
Tanks 4 12 heavy 1 a vehicle, reach and hits by its fire control (below) —
Infantry fighting vehicles 3 14 light 875 yards (800 m), 2 a vehicle, hits 70/45/20% 7 men
Armoured carriers 3 14 light machine guns only 10 men
Gun tractors and trucks 2 12 soft machine guns only tows 1 gun
Lorries 2 14 soft machine guns only 20 men
Ontos (106 mm recoilless rifles) 3 14 light 1,094 yards (1,000 m), 1 a vehicle, hits 75/50/25% —
  • Moving. Vehicles cross open and high ground at a hex for a hex, and rough ground, slopes and woods for more. They cannot enter marsh, buildings, rubble or water, so in a town they keep to the streets.
  • Their machine guns fire as a machine-gun team's, about one gun to a vehicle.
  • Main guns fire each exchange at the nearest enemy in range, in sight and in front, enemy vehicles first, with a clear line of fire. A tank's gun hits and reaches by its fire control, its war's unless the battlefield gives its own:
Fire control Reach Hits a vehicle (first round, at a standing target) Its wars
Optical sight 1,640 yards (1,500 m) 75% to 219 yards (200 m), 50% to 547 yards (500 m), 25% to 1,094 yards (1,000 m), 5% to 1,640 yards (1,500 m) WWII, Korea
Stadia reticle 1.2 miles (2 km) 98% to 547 yards (500 m), 35% to 1,094 yards (1,000 m), 4% to 1.2 miles (2 km) Vietnam
Laser rangefinder 1.9 miles (3 km) 98% to 547 yards (500 m), 94% to 1,094 yards (1,000 m), 75% to 1,640 yards (1,500 m), 55% to 1.2 miles (2 km), 35% to 1.9 miles (3 km) Late 20th century
Thermal fire control 1.9 miles (3 km) 98% to 547 yards (500 m), 94% to 1,094 yards (1,000 m), 75% to 1,640 yards (1,500 m), 55% to 1.2 miles (2 km), 35% to 1.9 miles (3 km) Iraq & Afghanistan
  • Armour. Small arms cannot hurt an armoured vehicle, and men armed only with them do not shoot at one. Trucks and gun tractors are soft-skinned: rifles and machine guns shoot at them too, every shot aimed, and each hit knocks one out at the chance below. No one fights a vehicle hand to hand.

Knocking them out

Rocket teams fire a round for every 4 men each exchange, and missile teams one for every 10. Every round is aimed, and range, cover and the weather count as for shots at men. Fired at men, a rocket is aimed at the hex and bursts there if it hits, striking each man in the hex as a tank's round does; in a building, a tank's round or a rocket bursts in the room and strikes each man there at half. A hit knocks the vehicle out at:

A hit from Heavy armour (tanks) Light armour Soft-skinned (trucks, tractors)
A rocket (RPG, bazooka, recoilless rifle) 15% 50% 80%
A guided missile 60% 90% 95%
A main gun 35% 75% 90%
A rifle or machine-gun bullet — — 5%
  • Where it is hit. A hit into the flank counts ×2, and into the rear ×3, to 100% at most. Which it is depends on where the shooter stands.
  • Composite armour (a battlefield gives it to the M1A1): as heavy armour, but a main gun's round from its front does not knock it out.
  • Morale. A vehicle unit's morale checks count whole vehicles lost, not crewmen hit in vehicles still fighting.
  • Damage short of that. A hit that does not knock the vehicle out strikes the turret at 35%, else the hull.
  • On the turret it puts the main gun out at 40%, and immobilises the vehicle at only 5%.
  • On the hull it immobilises the vehicle at 35%, and puts the gun out at 5%.

Immobilised vehicles can still turn. Their crews can abandon them and leave the fight unhurt. - Shells and bombs bursting in a vehicle's hex knock it out at the kind's own chance: a heavy howitzer's 2%, a fighter-bomber's 15%. Light armour is 3 times as likely to go, soft-skinned vehicles 6 times. - Knocked out. Its crew are out of the fight. Each is struck at 50% and wounded as by shellfire; the rest bail out.

Anti-tank guns

In the Second World War and Korea, a unit can be anti-tank guns: towed guns such as the British 6-pounder, the American 57 mm, the German Pak 38 and 40, the Soviet and North Korean 45 mm and the Japanese 47 mm.

  • Crews. Each gun has 5 men. A gun fires while one of its crew is up, and its crews manhandle it 2 hexes.
  • Fire. Each gun fires 1 round an exchange, as a tank's main gun does. Out to 1,094 yards (1,000 m), it hits a vehicle at 70/45/20% (close, mid and full range), and the hit then knocks the vehicle out as a main gun's would. At men, its high explosive bursts as a tank's round does.
  • Towing. Gun tractors and trucks tow a gun each, the crews riding. Hooked up beside them, the guns move with the tractors and do not fire; unhooked, they fire from the next exchange.
  • Rounds. Each gun brings 40 rounds. A gun out of them is resupplied as a battery is: an exchange out of contact, neither moving nor firing.
  • Shields. Anti-tank and anti-aircraft guns have shields: small arms fired at them from in front lose 30%. Shields do nothing against shells or fire from the flank or rear. Some machine guns had shields too (a Maxim on a wheeled mount, say), though most did not: in set-up the GM can mark a machine-gun unit shielded, and it gets the same cover.
  • Vulnerable. Otherwise its crews are men: rifles, machine guns and shells strike them, and hand to hand they fight with bayonets.
  • Emplaced. Before the battle the GM can dig in any gun unit (anti-tank guns, anti-aircraft guns, machine guns or a battery). While it stands it counts as gone to ground, −15% and hidden, but it cannot move all battle, though it can turn. A unit that breaks leaves its pits.
  • The enemy commander tows its anti-tank guns forward and unhooks them in reach (see the enemy commander).

Minefields

From 1939, the GM can paint minefields before the battle, marked or hidden. A hidden field shows on the map only once something has gone into it. A unit that moves into minefield hexes sets them off before the exchange's shooting. The ground it crossed is reckoned along the cheapest way it could have gone within its move that crosses the fewest minefield hexes its side knows of, so a known field it went round is not set off; a hidden one on its way is.

Minefield Each man going into a hex struck Each vehicle going into a hex struck
Anti-personnel mines 10% —
Anti-tank mines — 30%
Mixed minefield 8% 25%
  • Men. A man struck rolls a wound as one hit by a mine, at 70%. Mine wounds fall mostly on the feet and legs.
  • Vehicles. A vehicle struck is knocked out at 25% (heavy armour) or 60% (light). Otherwise a track is blown off and it is immobilised.
  • Sappers. In set-up the GM can mark a foot unit as sappers. On its own side's move, before it moves and out of contact, it can start to lay mines of any kind or to lift them. While it works it neither moves nor fires. Moving, turning, breaking or coming into contact stops the work.
  • Laying takes 3 exchanges. Then the row of hexes just ahead of its front, as wide as its front, is a hidden minefield. Hexes where a unit stands are left clear.
  • Lifting takes 2 exchanges. Then the minefield hexes in that row that its side knows of are lifted: a lane.
  • The enemy commander sets its own sappers to work (see the enemy commander).
  • A side knows the mines its own sappers laid: its commander steers round them, and they do not strike its own men.

Riders

Infantry fighting vehicles, carriers and lorries carry men, and tanks carry 6 men on each hull. A foot unit beside them can mount if all its men fit and neither unit is in contact. Riders move with the vehicles. Men in an infantry fighting vehicle shoot through its ports (25% of them) and men on a tank's hull shoot from it (50%), at their own weapon's target; otherwise riders do not fight, shoot or check morale until they dismount beside them. When a carrier is knocked out, each of its riders is struck at 30%, as by shellfire. Lorries are soft-skinned: a rifle or machine-gun hit that does not knock one out strikes a man aboard. Men riding on a tank's hull are in the open: small arms shoot at the tanks for them, and each hit strikes a rider; shells bursting near the tanks strike them as men in the open.

For the GM

Armour is a problem the infantry must solve, not a fight it can win with rifles. Give the side without tanks rockets, anti-tank guns, mines, ground the tanks cannot cross, or the dark.

Night and the air

Fighting in the dark

The light limits how far anyone can see to aim or to call fire, as in Light: on a moonlit night 109 yards (100 m), on a dark night 55 yards (50 m). The weather's own limit still applies, and whichever is shorter counts. The dark also slows a march and turns men round:

Light Movement Losing direction
Daylight — —
Dusk or dawn — —
Moonlit night +1 a hex 10%
Dark night +1 a hex 25%
  • Losing direction. Each unit that moved in the dark may lose its way when its side's move ends. Its chance is the light's, adjusted by its quality: green +12%, regular +5%, veteran −3%. A lost unit ends a point off its line, a hex astray that way (unless that is blocked or touches the enemy), and cannot move next exchange, though it can turn.
  • Muzzle flashes. A unit that fires when the light limits sight to less than 328 yards (300 m) shows where it is. Through the next exchange, the hexes it fired from can be aimed at, and fire called on, from up to 328 yards (300 m) away.
  • Flares. A flare lights the ground within 109 yards (100 m) for 2 exchanges, and illumination rounds from mortars and guns light far more. A lit hex is seen as by day.
  • Night vision. From the 1960s, units can carry devices that see further in the dark. Vehicles carry their war's unless another is chosen: infrared searchlights in Vietnam, thermal sights from the 1980s on. No device sees past the weather's own limit, a sandstorm's included.
  • Infrared beams. A vehicle that fires in the dark by its infrared searchlight lights its target with a beam that enemy infrared sets, Starlight scopes and goggles pick up: through the next exchange, those enemies can aim at the hexes it fired from out to 1,094 yards (1,000 m). A thermal sight does not see the beam.
  • Washed out. A unit standing in a flare's or illumination round's light cannot use a Starlight scope, goggles or infrared set (its men see the dark beyond with their own eyes), and an infrared searchlight there shows no beam. Thermal sights are not washed out.
Device Sees to Aims at worst Through smoke
Starlight scope (1960s-70s) 219 yards (200 m) −15% —
Night-vision goggles (1990s on) 328 yards (300 m) −5% —
Thermal sight (tanks from the 1980s, teams from the 2000s) 656 yards (600 m) as by day yes
Infrared searchlight and sights (tanks, 1950s-70s) 175 yards (160 m) −20% —
  • Fixed lines. Before dark a machine gun can be laid on a fixed line. In the dark, with no target it can see, it fires blind down the line at an enemy within 1 hex of it, at −15%. The enemy commander, holding, lays its machine guns' lines by day or at dusk on the nearest enemy it knows of in reach, or else ahead toward one (or straight ahead) as far as it can reach and see, shifting such a line once onto an enemy that comes into reach off it.
  • The enemy commander knows only what its units see, so at night it waits for the enemy to come close or to fire.

Aircraft

Fighter-bombers and helicopter gunships are called like batteries; each "tube" is an aircraft. Fire can be called only where one of the side's units can see it fall.

Aircraft Comes An aircraft an exchange In all Scatter Struck % at 0, 1, 2 … hexes By night
Fighter-bombers (bombs, napalm) 2 exchanges after the call 2 bombs 4 3 hexes 45, 25, 12, 5, 2 no
Helicopter gunships (rockets, guns) at once 4 rocket and gun passes 24 1 hex 20, 6 yes
  • Weather. Aircraft do not fly in fog, storm, heavy snow, blizzard, sandstorm, and fighter-bombers do not fly at night. A mission called then waits until the weather clears.
  • Strafing and napalm. An air attack can be a strafing run or (fighter-bombers, from 1944) a napalm strip, flown along a line the GM chooses. Each pass covers 5 hexes strafing or 3 with napalm.
  • Strafing strikes each man there at 12%, less cover and for going to ground.
  • Napalm strikes at 45% and nothing protects. It puts a man down with critical burns, and kills 35% outright.
  • Marking the target. Smoke laid on the aimed hex before the aircraft arrive halves their scatter, as an air controller does.
  • Ground fire. After each attack run, every aircraft that attacked can be hit.
  • Small arms within 328 yards (300 m) of the aim: 0.5% for each machine gun served there, 1% for each unit with rockets, and 0.2% for every 100 men with other firearms, at most 12% in all.
  • Anti-aircraft guns within 1,094 yards (1,000 m) add 3% for each gun served.

Gunships fly low and slow, so they count it ×2. The whole is at most 35%. Of the aircraft hit, 40% are brought down; the rest are damaged and turn for home. - Air controllers. A unit can be given a forward air controller. When he can see the aim, the attack scatters half as far. Without one, aircraft will not attack within 109 yards (100 m) of their own men; the mission waits until it can.

Landing by air

From Vietnam on, units can come in by helicopter to a landing zone. Each side has so many helicopters: by default X-Ray's 16 Hueys of 5 men each, back for the next load 30 exchanges after they land. At the end of each exchange the free ones fly the lifts in the order called, at most 8 at a zone. The men land on the zone or the nearest spot within 4 hexes, and can move the next exchange.

  • Waved off. No one lands while an enemy unit stands within 2 hexes of the zone.
  • Turned back. Once the men of a unit already down have broken, the rest of its lift turns back.
  • A hot zone. If any enemy unit could shoot at the zone, each man landing is struck at 10% and wounded as by shellfire, and each helicopter is hit at 10%: 20% of those come down on the zone as a wreck, the rest go home damaged. Either way it is lost for the battle.
  • Supplies and extraction. A helicopter can set a supply dump down on a zone, and the helicopters can lift a unit out from near a zone (out of contact; it does not move while it boards). Its men flown out are safe.
  • A downed helicopter gives the men in its hex cover and is slow ground to cross.

For the GM

Night evens the odds against a stronger side, and its fire support and aircraft count for less in the dark. A defender with fixed lines, flares and a plan for illumination can still hold.

A later war: the squad

The medieval chapters followed one retinue. This chapter follows a US Army rifle squad in Vietnam through one night, with the same rules and, where dice are rolled, the dice given. The team builder made the squad.

The squad

The team builder rolls a rifle squad. David Martinez leads it: 3 terms, each a year of the war, so he is 21, with Command 50. Its machine gunner is David Jones, 2 terms, who fires the gun at 37% but defends at only 31%. Its grenadier is Daniel Davis, and its medic is David Martinez, Leechcraft 65. 5 riflemen follow them. Their kit: M1 helmet, nylon flak vest (US Army M1952/M69, 1952-75).

On the field map

The squad: an ambush in the dark

The squad lies in extended order beside a trail on a dark night, gone to ground. No one can see to aim past 55 yards (50 m). Shots at the squad lose 15% for going to ground, and only 10% of the aimed ones find a man to aim at.

An enemy column comes down the trail. When the squad's gun opens fire, its muzzle flashes give it away: the enemy can now aim at its hex from up to 328 yards (300 m). The sergeant calls the company's mortars for illumination. It lands this exchange and lights the trail as by day for 2 exchanges, so his riflemen can aim.

In the roller

The heroes' wounds are rolled in full, as in the fight.

The squad: the gun

An enemy rifleman, a regular, fires his AK at David at 50% and rolls 15: a margin of 35. Against a bullet, an arm takes a margin of 30 or more to be serious, so this one is serious. David dodges at 31% and rolls 40: no.

The round strikes his upper arm (right), where his vest does not reach. It bleeds 2, pain 2, and the arm is hurt. The wound carries shock, so he makes a stop check: Nerve 50, less 2 steps of pain, gives 30. He rolls 22 and passes: he fights on.

But the machine gun takes both hands. With an arm hurt he cannot fire it, as in Wounds, so he can only defend. At 1 Blood a round, his 17 Blood lasts 17 rounds.

The squad: the grenade

A grenade bursts beside Daniel. The thrower's margin is 25 (he rolled 25). A fragment in the body is serious from a margin of 10, so this is serious, in his chest (left). But his vest, a nylon flak vest (M1952, M69), takes 2 steps off a fragment: it is stopped. Against a rifle round the same vest takes nothing.

The squad: the medic

In a quiet moment David crawls to the gun. He binds David's arm at his Leechcraft 65 and rolls 12: he binds it, taking the bleeding down 2 steps to 0. The arm is still hurt (−20% to his attack with it), so another man takes the gun.

At dawn the squad carries him back. His wound goes onto the track as in Recovery.

For the GM

In a later war the heroes are the few men whose names the players know in a fight of hundreds. Keep the field map for the shape of the night and the roller for the moments that matter: a gunner hit, a medic crawling out, a vest that held.

Money by era

A Day is a common soldier's day's pay in his army's coin: the rules count in Days so that a price in 1415 and one in 2008 can be weighed against each other, but every price was set down in the money of its time, and the pages show that money first, with the Days after it. Where a coin has no soldier's pay to measure it by, its prices stand in the coin alone.
